item.title: UN Says Breaching 1.5C Warming Limit Is 'Imminent and Unavoidable'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, the UN has declared that exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit is "imminent and unavoidable." "We are now saying this window has closed, but we can open it again by making the overshoot as brief as possible," UN Environment Program Executive Director Inger Andersen said on a call with reporters. "This is about how to find a way back as shortly and as quickly as possible with as limited an overshoot as possible." CNN reports: Past reports have examined the distance between countries' emissions reduction commitments and what it would take to limit global warming to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels. However, this year's report redefines the gap. Instead, it examines new emissions overshoot scenarios, and what it would take to limit peak warming to just 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C before bringing temperatures back down to 1.5 C through emissions cuts and the use of carbon removal technologies.
The report makes clear that every additional fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5 C "raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation, and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts." Each added fraction of a degree of warming can have an "immense" impact "as measured in terms of damage, cost and loss of lives," said climate scientist Michael Mann of the University of Pennsylvania. Mann was not involved in producing the UNEP report.
According to the UNEP, which is based in Nairobi, the lowest overshoot scenario would keep peak warming to between 1.7 and 1.8 degrees C and return global average temperatures to at or below 1.5 C by 2100. However, to follow such a pathway, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to be slashed by far more than anything currently on the table at the upcoming COP31 talks. This would require an 18% cut by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.
Meeting this lowest-possible overshoot scenario would require a tripling of renewable electricity capacity by 2035, and dramatic cuts to fossil fuels, including the phaseout of coal by 2040, the report states. In addition, there would need to be a major scaling up of carbon removal technologies, which so far have not been proven to work at such a large scale. In stark contrast to these figures, the fulfillment of existing emissions reduction pledges would only yield a 5-to-8% emissions cut by 2030 and an 11-to-15% reduction by 2035, the report found. This would be associated with a peak warming of about 2.6 degrees C.
If countries simply follow their current policies, then warming could reach a peak of about 2.8 C. That estimate has increased since last year, in part because of the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and retraction of its emissions reduction commitments, the report states. Even the scenario that assumes countries meet their existing reduction commitments, and nations with net-zero pledges succeed in fulfilling them, still brings warming to a peak of 2.1 C.

item.title: Trump Hides IRS Report Showing How His Big Beautiful Bill Fucked America
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: It seems that burying reports because he doesn’t like the data within them is becoming a habit for Donald Trump and his administration. This practice didn’t begin during Trump 2.0, of course. He was burying reports he didn’t like all the way back in 2017. More recently, of course, a lot of the games being played to keep the public uninformed of actual information and data have occurred at HHS, where RFK Jr. is all too happy to simply hide data that doesn’t align with his conspiracy theories on topics like COVID vaccines or other medicines. But if Dear Leader wanted to crow about one thing, it would certainly be the economy. Even as we can see with our own two eyes how Trump policies have worsened the economic situation for millions of Americans overall, Trump’s public statements about the economy all revolve around how great it is, how it’s never been better, and how anyone saying otherwise is a communist illegal immigrant that hates Jesus…or something. President Trump’s pro-growth agenda has delivered strong economic momentum through tax relief, deregulation, and renewed private-sector investment. In 2025, inflation moderated, job creation accelerated, and consumer confidence rebounded as businesses expanded and wages rose. His America-First economic strategy is restoring prosperity, lowering costs, and positioning the United States for long-term growth.Unlike other matters of public policy, the economy is essentially math. And anyone who took math through high school will know that it’s not enough to solve the problem; you have to show your work. In this case, showing your work amounts to IRS reporting on the impact on taxation, filed annually after each tax season. But for some unknown reason, the Trump administration is blocking the release of that report this year.The data from the IRS was initially scheduled to be released in July and updated in September, but the agency hasn’t filed either, Politico reported Wednesday. The IRS claims it is still waiting for approval to release the figures from the Treasury Department. The data will reveal the real impact of Republicans’ tax policies—and whether they fell short of their promises.There are a couple of reasons that could be behind the delay in reporting. The most charitable of those, seriously, is that Trump’s tax-cut bill, the so-called Big Beautiful Bill, complicated the tax code so badly that the IRS is having a hard time actually gathering up and validating all the data it has. [One] possible explanation for the delay is that the many carve-outs and exemptions implemented by Trump’s 2025 tax cuts have potentially complicated the tax codes, so the IRS has more trouble producing the numbers in the first place.Could be, but I doubt it. Occam’s Razor does a lot of work for us here. The explanation requiring the fewest assumptions is also the most obvious: the report isn’t being released because Trump doesn’t like what it says. It also explains why the report hasn’t appeared despite it being months and months overdue. I have very little doubt that if we see this report, it won’t be until shortly after the midterm elections that are about to take place. Nina Olson, a former national taxpayer advocate, accused Frank Bisignano, the IRS’s chief executive officer, of purposefully withholding the data. “I think they are hiding stuff that doesn’t line up with all the crowing the CEO has been doing,” she told Politico.Data detailing which tax breaks were claimed by people in different income brackets and how much they paid in taxes could become embarrassing if it reveals that the tax burden shifted between income groups or that a suspicious number of people claimed certain breaks, Johnson told Politico.An explanation for what is going on here should be offered from the administration. Trump’s response would be enlightening. If we were in the economic “golden age” that Trump is constantly claiming we are, he should be doing everything in his power to get this report released before election day. He doesn’t appear to be doing so.And it’s pretty obvious why.

item.title: To Make Way For Data Centers, Google Will Pay Others to Use Less Power
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Google is funding one of the nation's largest "virtual power plants," paying homes and businesses indirectly to reduce electricity consumption during periods of peak demand so more grid capacity can be available for data centers. Under its expanded deal with Voltus, the program could provide up to 1,070 megawatts in the Mid-Atlantic PJM grid -- roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. The New York Times reports: That electricity won't come from new power plants. Instead, Voltus will sign up homes and businesses and give them financial incentives to curb their usage when local power demand is high or the grid is strained. Many of these reductions could occur automatically, such as through smart thermostats that dial back air-conditioning during peak summer hours or batteries that can provide temporary on-site power.
Each of these tweaks frees up only a small amount of power on its own. But by aggregating them across thousands of businesses and homes, Voltus says it can reliably provide lots of extra capacity when it's most needed, and do so within a few years. While tech companies will likely ultimately need to build traditional power plants if they want to keep building large data centers, this approach could be a faster, cheaper and less-polluting option in the interim. "We really see virtual power plants as a critical short-term solution," said Ellen Zuckerman, head of energy market development for North and South America at Google. "It's a way to invest in our communities, really double down on our clean energy ambition, but also meet capacity at speed and scale."

item.title: The Metric Is Not The Mission: After The Platform Age
item.author: Konstantinos Komaitis
item.content:encoded: The Metric Is Not the Mission is a ten-part examination of how Big Tech moved from building and expanding the open internet to increasingly shaping it around its own metrics, incentives and assumptions. Across the series, the argument follows the evolution of the platform economy—from the optimism of the early internet to the growing tensions around power, prediction, geopolitics, accountability and the future of digital life.The series was published in two parts each week over five weeks, with each installment building on the one before it. The series is now concluded. The complete essay will be brought together in a single PDF edition, providing the full argument in one place, published shortly.Part X: After the Platform AgeThe final part brings the argument together. The question is no longer simply what comes after Big Tech, but whether the future of the internet can be built around a different distribution of power, one in which technological scale is matched by accountability.There is a revealing moment in almost every period of historical transition when people begin asking the wrong question. What comes after Big Tech? Will artificial intelligence displace social media? Will decentralized technologies restore the openness of the early web? Will new regulatory frameworks fragment today’s digital giants? Will smaller online communities replace planetary platforms?These are important questions, but they all assume that the future consists primarily of finding a new set of dominant actors. History encourages a different perspective. Periods of profound transformation are seldom defined simply by who inherits power. They are defined by changes in the architecture through which power is organized.That is why the coming reckoning should not be understood primarily as a prediction that today’s largest technology companies will collapse. Some may become even larger. They will continue investing in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, robotics, and other technologies that will shape the next generation of innovation. The more important question is whether the terms of their power are beginning to change.For much of the platform era, users were treated primarily as consumers. Governments treated the companies primarily as markets requiring regulation. The companies themselves treated social harms largely as problems of product design, trust and safety, or compliance.The emerging challenge is different. It asks whether users are also rights-holders. Whether platforms are also institutions with duties that cannot be reduced to terms of service. Whether corporate responsibility can be determined solely by what a legislature has explicitly required. And whether an industry that has become central to social, economic, and political life can continue insisting that responsibility ends wherever existing regulation currently stops.These questions may ultimately prove more consequential than another attempt to identify the next dominant technology. Because the future of the internet is not simply a question of which company wins. It is a question of whether the people who depend upon digital systems have meaningful power over the institutions that shape their lives. This is where the original architecture of the internet remains relevant.The internet’s greatest achievement was not that it prevented concentrations of power. It did not. Nor was it that it eliminated conflict, inequality, or abuse. It did none of those things. Its achievement was that no single institution was supposed to become synonymous with the network itself.That principle now needs to be recovered in a different form. Not by imagining that the internet can return to an earlier age or by romanticizing decentralization. And, certainly, not by assuming that technological innovation alone will correct the problems technological power has created.The next internet will require something more difficult: institutions capable of correcting one another. That includes legislators, regulators, and competition authorities. It includes courts. It includes civil society and independent researchers. And, most importantly, it includes users themselves. The point is not to weaken technology for the sake of weakening technology. The point is to ensure that technological power remains answerable to the societies in which it operates. That is the distinction that matters. The alternative to Big Tech is not necessarily small tech. The alternative to concentrated power is not the absence of power. It is accountability.Perhaps that is the real reckoning now approaching. Not the collapse of the platforms, not their sudden repentance or, the moment when their founders rediscover the idealism of the early internet. The reckoning will come when the companies discover that scale is no longer sufficient to define the terms of responsibility.Child safety may be where that process becomes impossible to ignore. It should not end there. If the emerging principle is that powerful technology companies can be held responsible when their products create foreseeable and preventable harms, then that principle must eventually extend to the wider question of what users are owed. Not only safety – but agency. Not only protection – but dignity. Not only compliance with the law as it currently exists – but accountability proportionate to the power these companies exercise over the conditions of modern life. That is not an argument against innovation. It is an argument against the increasingly implausible belief that innovation exempts powerful institutions from responsibility.For a generation, Big Tech invited us to believe that the future of the internet could be contained within a handful of platforms. Those platforms transformed communication, knowledge and human connection in ways that deserve recognition as some of the most consequential technological achievements of modern times. But achievement is not immunity. The internet was never Facebook; it was never Google; it was never Amazon; it was never Instagram, TikTok, or X. Those companies shaped an era. Some will continue to shape the next one. But the internet has always been larger than its most powerful inhabitants.The next chapter may be defined by something even more important than technological change: the reassertion of the principle that those who use the internet are not merely the raw material from which platforms create value. They are the people to whom those platforms must ultimately answer. That is the reckoning. And this time, Big Tech may not be able to lobby its way around it.Konstantinos Komaitis, PhD, is a veteran of developing and analyzing Internet policy to ensure an open and global Internet.

item.title: Microsoft Says October Updates Didn't Actually Fix VPN Issues
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
joshuark shares a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft says it mistakenly flagged a bug causing Always On VPN connection issues as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates. Always On VPN replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID-joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server. It runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network whenever their device connects to the internet.
Microsoft first acknowledged the issue in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying it was triggered on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later after installing the September 2026 security updates when the initial Always On VPN connection failed (e.g., when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed," it said. "In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'"
After releasing the October 2026 Patch Tuesday Windows 11 cumulative updates, Microsoft marked the bug as resolved, but in a Tuesday update it said the issues weren't actually addressed and that a fix would ship later. "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated," it said in a service alert sent to IT admins. "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks. We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." While Microsoft continues working on a permanent solution, it shared a temporary fix that requires affected customers to choose one of two VPN tunneling protocols to work around the issue.

item.title: Portal Texas Used to ‘Rubber Stamp’ Data Centers Down After 404 Media Reporting
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Texas has for its automated construction permit filing system and suspended construction permits of 17 data center projects. The change came that a group of Texans discovered the state had continued to issue construction permits related to data centers despite Governor Greg Abbott calling for a pause in September.On Monday, the watchdog groups FracTracker Alliance and published reports detailing more than two dozen permits issued to Texas data center projects. On Tuesday, the website for STEERS – an application filing system for construction projects run by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) – returned a 404 error.By Wednesday, the site had this message on it: “TCEQ’s electronic filing application used for automatic authorizations has been temporarily shut down to ensure all applications are reviewed by agency staff to determine if they are related to data centers.”Before TCEQ shut the portal down, 404 Media viewed 17 different permits related to data center projects and saw that they’d been moved from “active” to “suspended” in the TCEQ central registry. “STEERS is a portal that TCEQ uses to rubber stamp construction approvals,” Sam Law, a researcher at FracTracker Alliance told 404 Media. “It seems like they forgot about it and the portal has been quietly issuing approvals since the governor’s order for a pause, including for OpenAI and Amazon this Monday and Tuesday.”The 17 suspended permits are related to stormwater construction, an approval that allows construction companies to raise and level ground. It’s a key, and sometimes final, part of the approval process for any construction project in Texas.“Now they’ve taken the unprecedented step of suspending 17 approvals and taking down the whole site as they switch to a more involved human review process,” Law said. “The irony is not lost on me. When fighting the AI data centers build out, it’s nice to have a clear example of how some work is better left to humans.”Law said he reached out to TCEQ and didn’t hear anything from them. The commission also didn’t respond to 404 Media’s request for comment. “I am very concerned that since contractors are accustomed to this automated approval process, they might not be aware of the suspension and continuing construction at some of the largest hyperscale facilities in Texas,” Law said.

item.title: Starlink Throttling In Ukraine Again Shows Musk’s Right Wing Extremism Is A National Security Threat
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Now the problem has popped up again, this time with a report that Musk pressured the Trump administration to throttle Ukraine’s Starshield (the military version of Starlink), undermining Ukraine’s ability to communicate and engage in military drone operations. Musk is a cornerstone of a well-funded global authoritarian alliance and, like Trump, wants global authoritarians to succeed. Both Trump and Musk are upset with Ukraine’s efforts to target Russian oil production facilities (in part because even higher domestic gas prices threaten Republican midterm success, and the success of Musk’s unrelenting assault on democracy and foundational civil rights):“Both Musk and President Trump have expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices. Last week, Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the people said, rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless.”Just a week earlier both Trump and Musk vacillated between pretending they didn’t know what was happening — to each trying to blame the other for the slowdowns, with Reuters originally insisting that the order to throttle Ukraine’s Starlink connections “came from the White House.” Regular Starlink terminals have automatic network throttling protection if a connected vehicle operates in excess of 70 km/hr. Starshield, in contrast, is supposed to have no cap, but has been throttled if drones or vehicles exceed speeds of 90 km/hr. The throttling reduced Ukraine’s ability to use the network for both offensive and defensive drone operations, causing “tens of millions of dollars in losses,” Ukraine officials said. At his right wing propaganda website formerly known as Twitter, Musk also tried to claim the order came from the White House:But the Wall Street Journal’s reporting indicate that many sources believe the decision to throttle Ukraine’s connectivity ultimately came from Musk himself:“During the uproar, SpaceX representatives called White House counterparts seeking a unified understanding and subsequent message that the company and Trump administration coordinated ahead of Musk’s directive, the people said.Some U.S. officials say that Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump didn’t specifically order any retribution against Ukraine. But a person familiar with the situation said Musk talked to multiple senior administration officials, including with Trump, before imposing the new speed cap, which Ukrainian officials said had allowed Russian missiles to evade their defenses.”Trump has repeatedly feigned ignorance, as recently as Monday insisting “I don’t know who it was, but I’d like to find out.” The stage play is for the benefit of the dwindling number of Reagan-era Republicans who (correctly) find a U.S. alliance with Putin to be traitorous. Secretary of Defense head Pete Hegseth tried to falsely claim that Ukraine somehow violated Starlink’s terms of service:“We haven’t pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that,” Hegseth told reporters, adding that “we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success.”Ukraine says their satellite connectivity is still throttled, imperiling operations. Ukraine’s relationship with Trump has soured (further) in recent weeks after the White House temporarily suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Trump’s also been broadly criticized for suspending Russia sanctions and greenlighting diesel imports from Moscow, something he apparently hoped would lower U.S. gas prices and save him from an expected midterm lashing for Republicans. Obviously the world’s richest man, and Trump’s biggest billionaire donor, unilaterally making decisions that prevent a U.S. ally from defending itself from authoritarian aggression is positively grotesque. As is the non-transparent game of patty cake and finger pointing in the wake of the decision. As is any telecom provider leveraging its monopoly to exert this level of political control. Musk’s decision to arbitrarily throttle Ukraine’s Starlink usage appears largely to be an act of ideological and financial self-interest. Higher gas prices mean midterm trouble for Musk’s preferred global ideology (authoritarianism dictated by the whims of mad oligarchs). Trump and Musk are also trying to drive Kyiv to the negotiations table with an eye on ceding significant territorial control to Putin. Republican control of the White House has been immeasurably valuable for Musk. Not only is Starlink now tightly woven to military operations and funding, but a Republican rewrite of the 2021 infrastructure bill is driving what could be billions in taxpayer subsidies into the back pocket of the billionaire for Starlink service he had already planned to deploy without subsidization. You’d like to think that future U.S. administrations realize that Musk is a very clear national security threat and act accordingly. You’d also like to think Musk’s extremism drives the evolution of more robust competition in the fledgling LEO satellite space. Preferably before Musk’s global authoritarian alliance completely dismantles what’s left of representative democracy worldwide.

item.title: Moderna Shares Plunge After Leak of Cancer Vaccine Data
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Moderna shares plunged as much as 25% after partial clinical trial data leaked for its personalized cancer vaccine developed with Merck, despite the full results showing promising outcomes for melanoma patients. Analysts attribute the selloff largely to inflated investor expectations rather than disappointing clinical results. CNBC reports: The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone. The data also showed the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy. The companies say about 82% of patients who received the personalized cancer vaccine alongside Keytruda were alive without their melanoma returning at two years, compared with 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
[...] Investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used in other forms of cancer in the future. It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus. "We assert this relative reduction in recurrence/death is clinically meaningful," said BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman. "Such a reaction likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy."
UBS analysts said "this is overall a strong data set" and gives more confidence in upcoming studies of the vaccine in kidney and bladder cancers. They added the stock reaction may be due more to massive expectations than disappointing data.

[...] This is hardly Bose's first audio acquisition (though it may be the most mainstream). "What does the brand stand for? Does it have meaning for consumers? Is it relevant to a group of consumers that, frankly, we otherwise aren't reaching?" Bose CEO Lila Snyder tells WIRED. "If you think about McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Skullcandy, they all fit into that realm. Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we're largely missing with the Bose brand."
That's why Bose has no plans to relocate Skullcandy from Park City, Utah, which Snyder says is the epicenter of board sports culture. "We want to make sure we're right at the heart of it, as they always have been," she says. Skullcandy products are also affordable, especially compared to other Bose products and Bose-owned brands, which lets Bose compete at both ends of the market.

item.title: JD Vance Says Trump Hates People Cashing In On Government Access. Meet Former Trump Lawyer Alina Habba’s $50 Million Contract.
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: On Wednesday, JD Vance did the one thing JD Vance knows how to do with full commitment: lie through his teeth about something he fully knows is bullshit. In this case, claiming that Donald Trump “hates the idea of people enriching themselves fraudulently over access to the government.”Perhaps JD Vance means that Trump is fine with Trump enriching himself via public office… but “hates the idea” of others taking money that should be going directly to Trump himself.And there’s now a story that can be used to test Vance’s claims. It involves Trump’s former personal lawyer, Alina Habba, who he tried and failed to appoint as a US Attorney (she held the position temporarily until a court said she was illegally appointed) and who was accused in a lawsuit of conning a former Trump golf club worker into signing an illegal NDA by posing as a neutral ally rather than someone looking out for Trump. A bombshell NY Times report reveals that the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a billionaire desperate for a pardon, gave Habba a $50 million contract, and the pardon soon followed. Not surprisingly, Habba insists the two things are unrelated, but come on.We’ve talked in the past about the idea of “soft corruption,” where even the mere appearance of potential corruption massively diminishes trust in government. Here, it’s difficult to see how the “soft” modifier even applies.The article points out that he hired a different former Trump lawyer, Chris Kise, as well as donated $3.5 million to a Trump PAC directly, but it wasn’t enough to secure a pardon (he did get a very light plea deal — dropping federal bribery, conspiracy, and wire fraud charges in exchange for pleading guilty to a campaign finance violation — from the Trump DOJ, but he wanted a full pardon). So then the family turned to Habba, who was still occupying the US Attorney’s office in New Jersey (despite a court having ruled she was doing so illegally) when she signed the deal:Then the Herrera family hired Alina Habba, who had been one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers and at the time was an adviser at the Justice Department. They offered her $10 million a year for four years along with a range of bonuses. In total, including bonuses, she was guaranteed more than $50 million over four years, according to interviews and documents obtained by The New York Times.Under the agreement, Ms. Habba would become general counsel at Concord Partners, a company that Ms. Herreraset up in late October 2025in Florida. The company has no public profile and its business remains unclear even to some people associated with the Herrera business empire. Ms. Habba finalized her deal days after the company was registered, while she was still serving as U.S. attorney in New Jersey.Even if you want to argue that the contract itself is legitimate, the fact that she took it while serving as the US Attorney should ring all sorts of alarm bells.She formally began her work for Concord Partners on Jan. 1. Weeks later, Mr. Trump granted Mr. Herrera a full and unconditional pardon.By then, Ms. Habba was a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. She had an office at the Justice Department and a protective detail from the U.S. Marshals, a holdover from her time serving as the U.S. attorney in New Jersey.The sequence of events raises questions about how Mr. Herrera secured the pardon and who might have helped him. People familiar with Ms. Habba’s contract said they believed that she was brought in to help with Mr. Herrera’s push for a pardon and expressed surprise at the scale of the compensation.When a sitting US Attorney lands a $50 million contract from the family of a man seeking a pardon, and the pardon shows up weeks after she starts that new made up job (while still working for the DOJ in an advisory role!), that’s about as blatant as corruption gets.Part of the problem with not cracking down on corruption is that it invites ever more blatant corruption, while destroying whatever trust the public has left in government. When the public sees that people are going into public service to effectively get massively lucrative deals from criminals, it makes the entire government suspect.There has always been some corruption in the US government, but it was limited, and those involved at least tried to hide it. Those days are over, and the Trump/MAGA movement seems to be looting everything it can get its hands on while it can. But sure, JD, tell us again how much Trump “hates the idea of people enriching themselves over access to the government.”

item.title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP Is the Cyber Equivalent of an Unexploded Bomb
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
BBC technology editor Zoe Kleinman likens the recently discovered PHP security vulnerabilities to an unexploded bomb, writing, "The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb -- I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet." Although no successful attacks have been confirmed, the AI-assisted discovery of long-hidden flaws has triggered a worldwide security scramble, with websites taken offline as a precaution and administrators racing to deploy patches before attackers can exploit the vulnerabilities. From the report: The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit. One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult. [...] It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites -- but the news was leaked. From that point the clock started ticking.
As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site. "There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University. "How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers? Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out."
But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made. We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either. As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success. "We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, told the Today Program on BBC Radio 4. "We have enormous capability to handle these risks."

item.title: ICE Officers Who Ran Over Man Were Trying To Arrest Someone Who Had Been Dead For Years
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: Not that we really needed any more evidence of bad faith by ICE and the officer who decided to drive his car across a city street and into an adjacent parking lot for the apparent sole purpose of running over a fleeing migrant, but here it is anyway.As we covered last week, ICE officers deliberately ran over a fleeing man before issuing self-serving statements that not only didn’t tell the truth about the incident, but apparently didn’t even tell the truth about the backstory. To refresh your memory, here’s the footage of the incident ICE subsequently lied about, as captured by a camera owned by a nearby business: In this, you’ll see an ICE vehicle accelerate into the parking lot and run over Miguel Parra-Hernandez. This does not appear to be an accident. To make things even more suspect, ICE officers then moved the truck Parra-Hernandez was driving from the street where it was stopped to near the entrance of the parking lot, apparently hoping to shore up the narrative it had delivered to reporters earlier.ICE alleged in a statement that “Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”ABC13 reached out to an ICE spokesperson, who said agents were attempting to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who was their intended target.ICE alleges Mendoza-Cervantes entered the United States illegally from Mexico five times and had a final order of removal issued by a judge. The agency also alleges Parra-Hernandez is in the country illegally.The only demonstrably true part of this statement was the fact that the man had been “struck” by “an ICE vehicle.” But the vehicle had to cross a street, aim itself at Parra-Hernandez, and accelerate in order to strike him. At no point was the man “running in front” of an ICE vehicle, unless you consider being struck in the back by an ICE vehicle to be exactly the same thing as “ran in front.” And there’s no legitimate reason for moving the “suspect” vehicle to the parking lot, especially since the running over of a person had turned the entire area into a crime scene. And it a crime scene. Responding local officers appeared to believe it was. And their suspicions were echoed by local prosecutors, who are now publicly stating the running over of Parra-Hernandez was a criminal act. A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer appeared to intentionally drive a vehicle into a Mexican construction worker in Houston then fled the scene, a prosecutor said Wednesday, rejecting the agency’s claim the man stepped in front of the vehicle while running from authorities.[Harris County District Attorney Sean] Teare said ICE already had two detainees in the SUV — a Jeep Cherokee — when it ran over Parra Hernandez, and his office will get statements from both of them before making a charging decision, likely next week.His office spoke with Parra Hernandez on Tuesday in the hospital.“What I’ve seen so far indicates to me that this agent intentionally struck this person and ran him over,” Teare said.The other part of the ICE statement is equally meaningless. Any time ICE officers kill, maim, or engage in violence against people, officials always claim these were the inevitable result of ICE engaging in “targeted” arrest efforts. But plenty of cops — even some of the worst ones — can affect arrests without killing or injuring people, much less accelerating hundreds of feet to run over someone who is fleeing. When immigration agents struck a man with an S.U.V. in Houston over the weekend, they said they were chasing an undocumented Mexican man facing deportation and multiple criminal charges. But the photo they shared of their target was of a man whose family says he died almost a decade ago.That day, ICE released a photo of the man they said they were seeking and said he had not been captured.But Jamie Jimenez, of Dallas, said the man in the photo was her father and that he died in 2017. He plunged to his death from a cliff as he fled immigration agents near the southern border, she said.While there are some complicating factors here, including the fact that one suspect ICE may have been seeking used this dead man’s name as an alias, there’s little reason to believe ICE did anything more than search a database and self-issue an administrative warrant. First off, the name in the ICE statement is wrong. The photo it released appears to match the dead man: Jose Jimenez-Mendoza. The ICE used in its statement is close, but definitely isn’t the same: Jose Mendoza-Cervantes. The fact that Jimenez-Mendoza had faced the same criminal charges as the named suspect in the ICE statement — DUI and unlawful possession of a firearm — strongly suggests ICE didn’t do any due diligence and just decided to go after whoever it managed to find that had a name to the search results, rather than actually try to find the suspect to arrest. None of this would ever have come to light either if ICE officers had decided to operate like public servants, rather than rogue operatives who answer to no one. And if there’s body cam footage of this attempted vehicular manslaughter, odds are we’ll never see it. And that’s a big if. Chances are footage exists, even if the officers were equipped with the now-mandatory cameras. What’s undeniably true is that ICE officers ran over someone and that the footage of the incident very strongly suggests this act was deliberate. And all the government has now is an immigrant who wasn’t even on its radar facing multiple surgeries to repair his leg and another guy the government doesn’t even know the name of who managed to successfully flee the scene. What it doesn’t have is any legitimate arrest or anything that might justify its actions.

item.title: Several Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities Accidentally Posted To Public Kernel Mailing List
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative appears to have accidentally disclosed several unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities on the public LKML instead of the private security list, including two CVSS 9.0 flaws that could enable remote code execution through SMB Direct and KSMBD. "This seemingly was a mistake with Linux's second-in-command Greg Kroah-Hartman responding to each report asking about their submission to the public mailing list," adds Phoronix. The newly-disclosed vulnerabilities include: ZDI-CAN-33549 as a CVSS 9.0 scored vulnerability for SMB Direct remote code execution vulnerability due to integer underflow. For this one there is a patch in a Git branch of code intended for Linux v7.5 but now presumably will be expedited for getting to mainline.
ZDI-CAN-33774 as a KSMBD race condition that can lead to remote code execution. Another CVSS 9.0 rated vulnerability.
ZDI-CAN-33367 is a vulneravbility for skbuff skb_zerocopy in the network code that can lead to local privilege escalation. For this one Linux kernel developers received a security report from another source last week over the same issue and a patch is expected to be posted soon.
ZDI-CAN-34068 as a VMWGFX VMware graphics driver bug with an out-of-bounds write leading to local privilege escalation.
ZDI-CAN-34076 an uninitialized resource in the NVMET code leading to information disclosure.
ZDI-CAN-32005 was also posted to the mailing list a day prior for a search-domain TCP query stack buffer overflow leading to local privilege escalation.

item.title: Google Staff Resign In Backlash Over Its AI Contracts With Military
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from the BBC: Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use. The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so.
"Realizing my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity. [...] After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said. Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights." But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.
The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for. Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns. Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future." "Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added.
[...] Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticizing the company. "In principle I'm not allowed to criticize Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticizing." Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."
A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave -- but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard." Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]." "Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said. In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles."
"We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns -- ranging from business ethics to misconduct -- and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."

item.title: AI Is Changing Everything About Hacking. No One Knows What Happens Next
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs. The rhetoric has ranged from worried-but-measured (things are about to get weird), to run-of-the-mill advice like update your software and make sure you have two-factor authentication on, to about AI-powered attacks, to things like ‘the it lasted,’ to outright . To give you a sense of what I’m seeing, Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor and one of the most respected cryptographers in the world, “we’re in the part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the zombies and hope it slows them down,” and “so many people discovering that the whole Internet is dry tinder and the only thing keeping it from burning is the fact that teenagers haven’t found the matches yet,” Green is alluding to the fact that hackers and researchers driving AI tools and agents are getting better at finding and exploiting all sorts of bugs in important systems. I’ve also seen numerous AI employees, as mentioned, go full prepper, suggesting people pull money out of their bank accounts, disconnect from the internet, purchase shelf-stable food, hoard water, put money in gold and cash, and purchase hand-crank emergency radios.And all those posts came people using AI-powered tools found vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet. In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in (an Indian entity that provides website security certificates), (an alternative to PHP), (a software development platform), (media server software), (a cloud provider), (a coding agent platform), and several other companies and services, though, rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers , , and discovered using AI. Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a service that has wide insight into the general health of the internet, , “In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.” So much is happening, and so quickly, that it has been difficult for me — someone who has been reporting and editing stories on security and hacking for a decade — to fully understand what’s going on, to have a sense of what could happen next, or predict where this is going. And I think that that is largely where we are at the moment, as I am writing this. But it has become clear that AI, broadly defined, has fundamentally changed both offensive hacking and defensive cybersecurity. This is not because AI has become sentient or because human beings have lost control of it or because of “swarms” of “rogue agents,” but because AI is proving something that we have always known: much of the software that runs the internet, our devices, our accounts, and our lives is vulnerable, or out of date, or has security flaws that human beings never noticed, or was installed by someone at a company who left the company six years ago and has been replaced four times and no one knows how to find them now or how to update it. This doesn’t mean that all of the vulnerabilities that have been found with the help of AI have been obvious or trivial; skilled hackers and researchers, driving AI tools, seem to be better than humans alone at finding vulnerabilities. But, critically, AI and large language models have made it extremely easy to essentially brute force the internet; if every piece of software is a door, AI makes it exceptionally easy to turn turn the knobs of every door to see if it’s unlocked, even on buildings that human beings had never really bothered to try to open. What we are learning at an alarmingly fast pace is that not only are some of the locks easy to pick, in some cases the door is wide open or there’s a giant hole in the wall. The recent spate of people using AI to hack their internet of things devices to run new software shows that, in some cases, it takes essentially no expertise to actually use AI to hack something.Meanwhile, we've seen the rise of "abliterated" AI models that are designed to not say no and open weights models that can be used for pentesting and potentially offensive hacks without the guardrails that exist in many off-the-shelf commercial models. In a blog post explaining the PHP vulnerability discovery, OpenAI said the findings highlight “how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” OpenAI basically argues that it did all of this research ethically, and that its discovery opened a “Defender’s Window” that allowed governments and critical infrastructure to prepare for the disclosure of the bug. ‘Researcher finds bug, ethically discloses it to company, company fixes it’ is the preferred course of action in cybersecurity, but AI is shortening the window for all of this, is leading more people to do more research more easily, and is making both bug finding and bug fixing much faster. Whether those fixes are actually deployed by individual companies any faster is another, much more complicated question. The answer in many cases is, probably, no. AI is also making all of this much more unpredictable. The security company Chainguard was criticized for breaking the embargo on the PHP vulnerability disclosure because it posted fixes for the vulnerabilities several hours before it was officially disclosed. Critics, including the PHP Foundation, said this could have let attackers figure out how to exploit the issues before website owners had a chance to protect their systems. In a LinkedIn post, Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said that his company independently found the same bugs by typing “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP” into a frontier AI model. Amazon, meanwhile, said that it before the official disclosure. These facts raise questions about whether the bug was exceptionally easy to find, whether the AI models that originally found the vulnerabilities incorporated that information into the model somehow therefore making it easier for someone else to find, or whether there was a leak along the way from someone connected to the disclosure process. Any option is concerning.After the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were discovered, some infosec experts started calling this “Black October,” and highlighted the fact that the , the , and various governments around the world told people to patch their websites and services immediately, and to take down services that couldn’t be patched. , several Wikimedia services, and were all temporarily taken offline so that they could be updated. As has already suggested, one of the biggest impacts of PHP2Shell could be the fact that many historic websites can’t or won’t be updated, may be proactively pulled offline, might eventually be hacked, and might never come back. The link rot could be horrendous, and a lot of history could be lost. For such a high-profile incident, most of the actual impacts thus far have been related to the proactive patching or removal of potentially insecure websites, and we have not seen immediate, widespread exploitation of the bug. Various low-effort, LLM-developed exploits have been dropped online; many of them will not work. A “There isn’t an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability,” written by Elias Taylor, quickly went viral and was dissected on Hacker News, especially by people pointing out that the website eliastaylor.com had been recently registered and that it wasn’t clear who Elias Taylor was. 404 Media reached Taylor by Signal; he said “I am real and on a delayed train.” “Lots of people are being tricked by AI into thinking they have an exploit when they don't, because they can't read or understand what the LLM gave them,” Taylor told 404 Media. “It doesn't appear to be anywhere near as exploitable as the other ‘stop the world’ vulnerabilities i.e log4j, heartbleed. But patch your servers, it’s still a vulnerability. Please do not paraphrase me as saying ‘there is no vulnerability’ for any reason. There is, and people should patch.” Dan Guido, the CEO of Trail of Bits, a well-respected cybersecurity company that partners with OpenAI initiative, had created “a working exploit,” and that “Will Tan built it in 1 day with Codex, drawing on ~10 years of system security and vulnerability research. AI accelerates exploit development. Knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise. AI makes that expertise more productive.” It should also be noted that Taylor’s is called “Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces,” which includes the lines “software engineers have spent the past 40 years writing vulnerable, dogshit software. LLMs are easily above the bar needed to break into said software.” It remains unclear, at the moment, what the ultimate impact of all of this is going to be, or where we’ll be in one hour, one week, one year, or 10 years. But AI is changing how cybersecurity and hacking works. It is making finding and exploiting bugs faster and easier. We’re about to find out how insecure the internet really is.

item.title: AI Is Already 'Amplifying the Destruction' of War
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: The UN met this week to discuss, among other things, the threat of autonomous weapons.“The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning,” Laurent Gisel, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) legal warfare team, told 404 Media. Gisel was in NYC this week to address the UN about all the things that are the planet. His prepared remarks include a statement on the illegal arms trade, nuclear weapons, mines, and – of course – AI.But the UN has pressed forward. On Tuesday, the international governing body announced a new initiative that would grapple with the issue. But, as Gisel said: “multilateral processes take quite some time” and “we already see the effects on the battlefield.” AI is already picking targets and killing people. Gisel said the technology is “amplifying the destruction, amplifying the violation of the law, amplifying the humanitarian harm caused by conflicts.”Israel used an AI powered by Microsoft to . In Ukraine, AI-powered Russian drones are deciding which humans to kill. The United States military is pitching itself as an “AI-first” fighting force. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth recently announced Project Meridian, an initiative to guide the AI-powered autonomous weapons of the future. Three of Meridian's leads are Elon Musk, defense contractor Palmer Luckey, and Newt Gingrich.For Gisel, one of the biggest dangers of AI is how fast it is. A core selling point for the tech is that it can help commanders make decisions faster. But that also accelerates the pace of mistakes. “Targets are created at higher speed and higher frequency, and are actually then prosecuted quicker, and with that give us great concerns in terms of the level of human control that is retained,” he said. “The human is supposed to remain in the loop.”The human does not always remain in the loop. The Israel Defense Forces told journalists it the kill lists generated by Lavender, the AI system it used to pick targets in Gaza. “It's known in the [civilian world] [...] that humans tend to trust the systems,” Gisel said. “That it's more the case when the humans are tired, when the humans are under stress, when the humans have to deliver quickly, and that's of course exactly the situation in which soldiers are in. So all of that gives us a lot of concerns in terms of retaining control on the use of force in armed conflict.”AI boosters often pitch AI as an “easy button,” a way for people to brute force a complicated task and get it over with. But the consequences are much different when someone in Silicon Valley is parsing spreadsheets or than when they’re prosecuting a war in the Middle East.“That's something that the developers of those systems don't necessarily realize either, because some of those systems are developed by technological companies very far away from the battlefield, and they are not naturally all developed for battlefield use,” Gisel said.International humanitarian law is an ever-evolving legal negotiation between world powers meant to limit the devastating effects of war. It’s imperfect and countries with vast armies like the US and Russia often do not abide by it. The ICRC, which Gisel represents, exists explicitly to shape these rules and laws. Some of the laws are old, far older than AI, but according to Gisel humanitarian law applies to “all weapons, means, and methods of warfare. Those of yesterday, those of today, and those of tomorrow.”Beyond the opportunity to code humanitarian law into AI, Gisel said there should be new rules and regulations for the new technology. “Not to prohibit them all, but to prohibit specific categories of autonomous weapon systems and put specific restrictions on others,” he said."...Once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle"But he does have redlines. The first is any AI support system that removes a human being from the kill chain. “That requires specific limits and guardrails and restrictions from our perspective,” he said.“The other type of autonomous weapon system that we recommend prohibiting is those that would target human beings directly, where the target profile is the human being, as opposed to a tank, weapon systems, or another typical military objective, and the reason why is based on ethical concerns, humanitarian concerns, and a moral line,” he added.Autonomous weapons have existed for a long time. Some US warships have gatling guns that track and destroy incoming targets automatically. The difference is that those weapons track ships and missiles, not human beings.According to Gisel, one problem with autonomous weapons that target humans or AI support systems that pick targets is that they’re unpredictable. He said banning unpredictable weapons should be a non-brainer. “Military discipline is about your forces [...] delivering the commander's intent,” he said. “If you have a weapon that is unpredictable in its effect, how can you deliver the commander's intent?”But it’s been a sticking point in negotiations. “We would have thought, military considerations, would align. But actually, that has also faced quite some pushback. Strangely enough,” he said. He spoke about the negotiations in August and September from earlier in the year. “There were references in the last proposal by the chair of the group on precisely all those questions: that the autonomous weapon systems need to be reliable, explainable, understandable, and predictable. And all of that was taken out by some states.”Gisel also opposes AI in nuclear command and control. In 1983, the Soviet Union’s early warning systems reported that the US had launched a nuclear weapon at the country. Soviet lieutenant colonel Stanislav Petrov decided the computer had made a mistake and decided not to report the attacks up the chain. He was right.“States will continue to use satellite systems and therefore algorithms that go with those satellites,” he said. “But it's so important to ensure that it remains entirely under human control and a really meaningful human control.”While the UN deliberates and the ICRC wrangles with how to regulate all this, the wars continue and military forces continue to embrace AI. “That's why it's urgent to have decisions being made by the international community on what to prohibit and what to restrict [...] once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle,” he said.Gisel said the world needs to act now. “Otherwise, it's the technology that will decide what is acceptable, and that's not the world we want to live in, right?”

item.title: Brendan Carr, A Weak Coward, Threatens Journalists For Covering Polls Trump Doesn’t Like
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Lately Trump has been complaining about the numerous polls all showing that he’s historically unpopular due to stuff like covering up for a pedophile and launching a disastrous war that’s driving up the cost of living for everybody. Most polls show Trump’s likely to sink Republicans in the midterms. So like a dutiful little yipping chihuahua, Carr took to Elon Musk’s right wing propaganda website on Wednesday to once again hurl threats at journalists for the “crime” of…covering polling that clearly shows the U.S. President is historically unpopular:If you can’t read it, it starts with Carr making the false claim that there’s a bunch of fake polls circulating that journalists are unethically repeating en masse. This is silly fascist code for the fact that Republican internal polling data indicates Trump’s fading health and political power are going to be an albatross around their necks this midterm voting season:“During this election season, there has been a significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls designed to do nothing more than interfere with the regular functioning of the electoral process and alter the normal patterns of voter turnout and enthusiasm.Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis.”Carr continues by once again threatening to harass media companies for discussing polls the thin-skinned president and his pasty sycophants don’t like. He also, once again, falsely claims that he has the authority to act (read: censor media companies) under the FCC’s dated “broadcast news distortion” rule:The FCC takes these issues seriously. Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes. It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations. After all, the country benefits greatly when Americans can trust and rely on the media to report the news fairly and accurately.Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations. If broadcasters believe they should provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered, they can now take those actions consistent with FCC regulations.”This is Carr pretending to be important. He really likes when people are afraid of him and when the press talks about him. But as with his threats against ABC, this is an obvious violation of the First Amendment, an abuse of his office, and a giant turd of a legal case should he pursue it. It’s worth noting (and it’s not something most press coverage discusses) that one benefit of Carr’s endless censorship saber rattling is that it obscures how much damage he’s doing on issues like media consolidation and consumer protection, stuff the corporate press couldn’t care less about. The FCC’s broadcast news distortion rule, created in 1949, gives the agency the power to punish media companies for clear ethical violations involving an intentional, misleading distortion of “a significant event and not merely a minor or incidental aspect of the news report.”Ideally, this would be something like a media company taking a large bribe from a company or public official to kill a story. The FCC had only actually used the rule eight times between 1969 and 2019, and few of those actions actually resulted in serious, substantive punishment. It most certainly doesn’t apply to a right wing politician trying to censor news the President doesn’t like. A bipartisan array of former FCC officials recently pointed out that the rule should probably be eliminated altogether, as it inherently risks violating First Amendment principles, chills journalistic speech, and as Carr demonstrates is easily abused by radical extremists. In a statement, Anna Gomez, the FCC’s only Democratic Commissioner (because Republicans simply refuse to approve any others), reiterated that Carr’s threats are empty:“Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong. FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”These Carr threats worked initially because companies were afraid of the President — or at least really liked tax cuts and deregulation, and didn’t want to be subject to costly legal harassment. But as Trump’s political power wanes those threats will continue to hold less and less weight, and corporations (as we’ve seen with both ABC and the BBC) will start showing more and more backbone.You’d like to think Carr will be held accountable for his historic abuses of FCC authority and trampling of the First Amendment, but his most likely fate remains a high six figure gig at some telecom industry think tank where he comfortably spends the rest of his days finding creative ways to reduce competition for the large companies (AT&T, Comcast, Securus) he’s very clearly captured by.

item.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.

item.title: Startup Claims To Use AI-Created Viruses To Treat a Patient
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: For the first time, scientists say they have used viruses designed by artificial intelligence to treat a human patient. Researchers announced on Tuesday that they had administered the virus, known as a phage, to a patient suffering from a deadly bacterial infection. Phages attack bacteria, and the hope is that this one will kill the microbes causing the infection. Radical Numerics, the start-up that created the viruses, posted a technical report about them on its website. But the company declined to provide information about the patient or the doctors running the trial, citing confidentiality requirements.
[...] In 2025, researchers at the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, Calif., created an A.I. model called Evo 2, which they trained on millions of DNA sequences, including phage genes. They prompted Evo 2 to make new genomes similar to those in a group of phage species. The A.I. generated 700,000 virus genomes. The team synthesized DNA molecules from 285 genomes and inserted them into bacteria. The researchers found that 16 of the genomes gave rise to viable viruses. Three members of the Evo team, including Dr. Nguyen, left to found Radical Numerics. In June, the company unveiled a new A.I. model, called Omnii, based on some of the same principles as Evo.
Omnii can be trained not just on DNA but also on other aspects of biology, such as the structures of proteins and molecules that keep genes turned on or off. The company is now using Omnii to tackle a range of challenges, including designing cancer vaccines and recognizing the risk that a virus may cause a pandemic. Among these efforts is the first trial of A.I.-designed phage therapy. The researchers created variations of a phage called T7. The virus, which only infects E. coli, looks like a microscopic Apollo lunar lander: a ball-shaped protein shell that holds its DNA atop six leglike protrusions. To infect a bacterium, T7 lands on its surface, using its legs to anchor in place. It then injects its DNA into the cell.
Omnii generated new viral genes altering the shapes of T7's legs, according to Dr. Nguyen and his colleagues. While some of the new legs were significantly different from natural ones, Omnii's phages could still infect bacteria. Once the researchers were confident their strategy had worked, they partnered with doctors treating a patient with a stubborn E. coli infection. The bacteria had resisted not just antibiotics but all the available phages. The researchers said they had trained Omnii with information about the resistant strain and told it to design T7 phages with legs that could grab onto the bacteria. Once the A.I. generated genomes for new viruses, the scientists said they produced the corresponding DNA molecules and inserted them in bacteria. The bacteria became infected and produced T7 phages that could successfully infect, and kill, other microbes. After running tests to make sure the phages were safe, Radical Numerics presented them to the doctors. The F.D.A. authorized a trial. While the trial was authorized by the FDA, it's worth noting that the research has not yet been peer-reviewed in a scientific journal and there's no guarantee the AI-designed phages will work.
However, if it does prove successful, it could help speed phage therapy by cutting down the time it takes to create a new virus tailored to each patient's infection. "We think we can get it done in days," said Dr. Eric Nguyen, the chief executive officer of Radical Numerics.

item.title: Epic Rolls Out Vibe-Coded Launcher Update & It’s Absolute Trash
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: Alright, I don’t quite know what to make of what Epic Games is doing with this AI-driven nonsense, but it’s not great. I’ve spent a bit of time trying to argue that new AI technology has some place in this industry, but Epic and its leadership appears to be trying to personify every last thing the never-AI-ers state they’re worried about. First it was Tim Sweeney trying to argue that Steam’s AI disclosures are “irresponsible“, which is so obviously stupid that it hardly needs a retort. Then, more recently, Epic’s leadership messaged to its own internal developers that use of AI is not a potential useful option, but is compulsory and mandated. It seems Epic wants to be the corporate goon the naysayers have said to watch out for. And with the company pulling this kind of shit, it gets harder and harder to argue with them.“Programming is hard,” the company wrote in its official announcement post for a newly released preview version of a revamped launcher for the store. “So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look. This first release is light on features. Think of it as a speedboat and not a yacht! Though it does have advanced digital commerce technology such as a shopping cart.”“We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy,” the Epic X account posted. “Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview.” It was accompanied by a graphic showing that the genAI storefront performed faster on certain responsiveness benchmarks than Valve’s competitor. This isn’t just a stunt or a flex for AI boosters on Elon Musk’s social media platform, though. The adults at Epic aren’t joking about wanting to make its storefront more appealing.Indeed, while some of the messaging about the new launcher was obviously tongue in cheek, Epic didn’t release this new launcher as a joke. Which is incredible, given just how much of the internet is laughing at them over it anyway. Other reactions on the wider internet span the range of “lmfao” and “hahahaha” to “please don’t tie any of your actual payment or credit card information to whatever this giant piece of shit is.” If all of this was meant to poke Valve’s Steam storefront in the eye, it backfired spectacularly.Particularly, as others have pointed out, since Epic still relies on Valve to do other things it can’t seem to do:Epic also announced that it’s bringing Fortnite to Linux via Proton, a compatibility layer made by, surprise, Valve. “Bold of them to sh*t on Valve/Steam, and then literally use Proton internally for Windows compat on Linux…,” one VR modder wrote on X. “This launcher is so fucking vibeslopped its funny, but holy crap, these people are hilarious.” A Twitch streamer wrote in the comments beneath Epic’s announcement, “Are you seriously incapable of embarrassment? I’m not leaving Steam for this trash.”If you think AI has a place in the industry, this is all the ammunition the other side of the argument needs, honestly. It might as well be gift-wrapped to the never-AI crowd. If you are in that never-AI crowd, it seems Epic is trying to make all of your Christmases come at once.This . That Epic is trying to boast over this level of suck is perplexing.
