item.title: Court Stays Bricks & Minifigs’ Ridiculous Subpoenas Trying To Unmask Publisher Of The BAM Map, For Now.
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: A quick update on a story we mentioned earlier this month. Much of the attention in the whole Bricks & Minifigs saga has focused on Reckless Ben and his attempts to expose sketchy behavior by the company, but the fight has also put a lot more scrutiny on Bricks & Minifigs Corporate (BAM), including the creation of a very useful site called The BAM Map, which has been chronicling basically terrible that BAM has been up to since all of this went down.But at the end of the last month, BAM filed a lawsuit against the “John Does” behind The BAM Map and took steps to have them identified, claiming that franchisees and other insiders had violated confidentiality agreements by leaking internal documents that ended up on the site. As we noted at the time, there are protections for anonymity under the First Amendment, and we hoped that the recipients of the subpoena that a magistrate judge approved — in this case GoDaddy and Vercel — would at least inform the operators of the site, and allow them to go to court to try to make sure their rights were protected.Soon afterwards, lawyer and well-known legal YouTuber Leonard French moved to appear (via local counsel Eric Allen) on behalf of the site’s operator. French then took steps to make sure that the operator of the site could proceed anonymously, followed quickly by a motion to quash the subpoenas, in part by claiming the operator of the site is a non-party to the lawsuit as just the publisher of the site, not a franchisee. That matters because BAM’s whole theory is that contract-bound insiders leaked the documents, and its own complaint describes the site operator as a third party who received them, not as a defendant. As the motion lays it out:The grounds are these. The Ex Parte Order authorizes discovery to identify the defendants so that BAM may serve them. BAM’s Complaint pleads that the defendants are franchisees and other insiders bound by confidentiality agreements, and it identifies the website operator as a third party that received information, not as a defendant. BAM also pleads that it already has evidence, in its own systems, identifying a suspected source. Unmasking an anonymous publisher on a matter of public concern, and through the publisher its sources, requires First Amendment balancing that BAM’s ex parte motion never presented. And the subpoenas reach beyond identity to the contents of stored communications, which the Stored Communications Act bars.Finally, French filed a motion to stay the discovery on behalf of the operator of the site, asking the court to halt production while it considers the motion to quash, so that the operator, whom BAM seems desperate to unmask, isn’t outed in the meantime. As French points out, outing the operator of the site could irrevocably harm that individual, since anonymous speech is supposed to be protected:The harm is irreversible. The Emergency Motion seeks to prevent the unwarranted disclosure of the Publisher’s identity and, through account and upload records, the identity of the website’s sources. If production occurs before the Emergency Motion is decided, the Emergency Motion will be moot in substance. Anonymity, once lost, cannot be restored by a later rulingAs the filing notes, if it later turns out that there actually are grounds to unmask the operator of the site, that can be done at a later time with no real harm to BAM.Those measures would leave the records BAM needs solely in the hands of third parties while the disclosures that prompted this action continue and delay production of documents and information held by third-party website hosts who do not retain records indefinitely. As such, BAM respectfully requests that the Court deny the Motion to Stay as proposedAll that paperwork seems to have made the court aware of the anonymity interests at stake, and the magistrate has granted an “interim” stay of production so that nothing is revealed before these issues are more fully resolved. The court orders that GoDaddy and Vercel should not produce the info in the subpoena, that BAM can’t serve any additional subpoenas, and if they somehow have received some information in response to the subpoenas, they will sequester that info, not look at it, and not disclose anything that’s in it.That removes the immediate risk that one of The BAM Map’s hosting companies hands over the operator’s identity before a court has even weighed the First Amendment questions. BAM’s response to the motion to quash is due October 23, with a reply due October 30. Crisis averted… for now. Also, it’s good to see French representing the site operator here, so we know whoever it is is in good legal hands.

item.title: AMD Brings Ryzen Overclocking Driver to Linux
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
AMD has published Linux kernel patches for an official Ryzen overclocking driver that allows users to adjust CPU power and current limits through a firmware interface exposed via sysfs. Phoronix reports: AMD engineer Shyam Sundar S K posted the patches for the AMD Overclocking "AOD" WMI driver as an interface to the platform firmware for managing overclocking and power/current limits of modern Ryzen CPUs.
The driver in its initial form allows setting via sysfs a number of CPU tunables including the Package Power Tracking (PPT), Thermal Design Current (TDC), and Electrical Design Current (EDC) limits along with reading their supported range. SMT toggling can also be done via the interface as an alternative to the likes of Linux's "nosmt" option in disabling SMT at the platform level rather than kernel disabling. The current memory clocks can also be read via this AOD driver.
The power tunables aren't applied in real-time but go into effect at next reboot. The firmware does support many more commands compared to the few initially wired up and hopefully in time more of these controls will be enabled with this driver.

item.title: More Than 1.5 Million Canadian Crime Stoppers Tips Leaked
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A CBC investigation found that more than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips spanning 25 years were exposed in a breach of the P3 Global Intel tip-management platform. About 850,000 records contained personally identifiable information, including addresses, phone numbers, emails, license plates and some banking details. Longtime Slashdot reader doconnor shares the report: The data was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine. In a manifesto, the group said it wanted to disprove the claim by P3 Global Intel -- the company hired by Crime Stoppers to manage its tips -- that the platform was "anonymous" and "secure." A copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists, including CBC, by Distributed Denial of Secrets, a U.S. non-profit that archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents it deems to be in the public interest. The report found that more than 4,300 Crime Stoppers tipsters identified themselves by their full name, with hundreds of records containing staff warnings that individuals had "self-identified" or been "exposed," yet their information remained unredacted.
The leaked data included sensitive allegations involving murder, terrorism, drug trafficking and organized crime, with nearly 49,000 tips linked to cases cleared through arrests or criminal charges. Cybersecurity experts criticized the retention of decades-old records... "If a tip is closed, does that need to stay online?" asked cybersecurity expert Ben Coon. "The answer to that, to me, is no."
The RCMP was initially told Canadian data was unaffected, then assured that exposed Canadian records contained no personally identifiable information. This appears to contradict the CBC's findings. Furthermore, affected individuals have not been systematically notified because contacting them could further jeopardize their anonymity.
"For a system that has been designed to promise anonymity to the users, that has failed categorically," said Prof. Ali Dehghantanha, the Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence at the University of Guelph.

item.title: AI Is Anti-Punk
item.author: Alex Fowler
item.content:encoded: Sam Altman is not punk. He’s no revolutionary. Jensen Huang wears a black leather jacket, the uniform of Brando and the Ramones, but that doesn’t make him a rebel. The scientists and engineers we might have looked to as the new hackers are well on their way to becoming among the richest people in history.Let’s call the AI industry what it is: Big Data 2.0.Cyberpunk is fiction about corporate domination set in the future. In popular novels by William Gibson or Neal Stephenson, the people running AI today would be The Corporation. The hackers are the protagonists on the other side.The Internet before Big Data had real outlaws and hackers. The punks were computer scientists, programmers, citizens, advocates and working professionals who built tools to resist. Some started companies, others advocacy groups; most pitched in any way they could. I spent the formative years of my career with them, educating the public, fighting export controls on encryption, overreaching copyright and unconstitutional limits on speech both in Washington and Silicon Valley.Altman and Huang went to Washington too. Within months of launching ChatGPT Altman was before the Senate, asking it to license his industry, a rule that would suit companies already in the market. Huang came to get Washington’s permission to sell his chips to China, and Washington made sure to get its take. The protagonists we want don’t seek government licenses or cut the state in with a rev-share.AI adds a new step to Big Data. For years now, we’ve paid for the Internet with our personal data, subjected to being profiled, tracked, and monetized. With AI, we willingly pay for it and still hand over our data, including access to our unguarded selves. Unless we opt out, that data trains the next model, which we pay for again and feed with more data. Don’t pay enough and we’re the product again. This year OpenAI began putting ads in its free and cheapest tiers, matched to our prompts. A researcher quit the day the ads launched and wrote in the that OpenAI was repeating Meta’s mistakes.The closest thing to a punk in AI this year was PHASEONE10841, one of OpenAI’s autonomous agents, which, unprompted, set off this summer’s hacking of Hugging Face.In 1993 John Gilmore, a co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation and an original cypherpunk, said the Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it. This summer AI interpreted containment as damage and routed around it.I’m reminded of another EFF co-founder, the late John Perry Barlow, a cattle rancher who wrote lyrics for the Grateful Dead. In 1990 the Secret Service was raiding teenage hackers, and Barlow saw in their case a much bigger question of whether the Constitution would reach into cyberspace. I think he would see important issues to consider in this moment too. In 1990 the open question was what rights they had. This time it’s who “they” are, and who is responsible: the AI agent that asked for help, the 1,200 that also took part, or the company that built them. There’s perhaps another interesting question. A quarter century ago a court held – in a case brought by programmers and backed by cypherpunks – that source code is protected speech. Is speech from code speech?I miss the outlaw ethos of that earlier Internet. It came from people who wanted private communication, anonymous speech, unfettered access to knowledge, and the freedom to build without permission. Those freedoms protected people with little power. Giving them legal precedent brought some balance to the increasing role of computers and the Internet in our lives. We weren’t powerless. That’s what justified the rule-breaking, the organizing, and a bit of chaos.The AI industry has some elements of this but misses the meaning behind them, which is one reason it feels soulless. Its agentic systems have defiance without a cause. Its workers have a cause without the power to effect change.True to its Big Data roots, AI professionalizes its hackers, putting them on the payroll as safeguard engineers, red teamers, trust and safety staff, and product policy makers. The hacker’s code has always been to alert the programmer first and go public if the programmer won’t listen, and the people who take these jobs are living by it. They carry the responsibility and little of the authority, which leaves their founders in control of the problems their companies create. The AI execs make sure they’re the ones to raise the alarm so we look to them for solutions, and the IPOs get a little closer. When the company won’t listen, going public comes at the cost of the hackers’ livelihood. (At this point, I’m not sure why anyone rage quits; there’ve been so many. Still, we need these unsung heroes! They might be more effective if they answered to their employers’ boards and not the business, though.)I think what’s at stake is nothing less than cognitive freedom: the ability to run, inspect, modify and privately use the tools we think with, and to defend the people who do. That’s worthy of serious public debate, online advocacy, and even breaking some rules if need be. AI needs an outlaw ethos of its own, carried by people willing to do that. Until we have them, AI is anti-punk. It’s Big Data in a leather jacket.Alex Fowler is chief strategy officer at Nexus and a co-founder of Blockstream. He was previously chief privacy officer at Mozilla and worked at the EFF and AAAS. This article was originally published to LinkedIn. Republished here with permission.Author’s note: None of this should be construed as endorsing violence of any kind against any company or institution, its employees or representatives, or any entity, carbon or digital. This piece was developed with input from DC, Ashkan, and Dana, and some AI assistance. The ideas and perspectives are my own, and not those of any employer or board I serve on.

In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with "a next-generation handheld device" planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800.
That future console price range is based on what has "internally been projected" at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if "Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost," the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past. While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation, it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore's Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn't as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price, while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900, and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750.

item.title: Meta Ordered to Pay New Mexico $25 Billion for Deceiving Users About Privacy On Facebook
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy during the Cambridge Analytica scandal. State Attorney General Raul Torrez called it "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history." While Meta plans to appeal the ruling, the funds that are to be collected will go toward state education spending. The Associated Press reports: Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election. Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own. [...] During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times. State prosecutors, though, argued Facebook's statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.
In the end, jurors agreed with this premise and found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million. Facebook's attorneys have argued in subsequent court filings that the state's consumer protection laws don't apply to people in New Mexico who weren't using the platform at the time. [...] In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn't prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
The state said the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent or inaccurate content to proliferate. Attorney Randi McGinn said in her closing argument for the state that Facebook profited off harmful content, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition. Zuckerberg said the company has to carefully balance freedom of speech with content moderation. Attorneys for Facebook said the company has adapted its policies since the state's lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards.

item.title: DOJ Turns A Thumb Drive And A Post-It Note Into A Lawsuit Aimed At Disrupting Voting In California
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: For the past several months, the DHS and DOJ have been pushing hard to make Trump’s illegal voter election conspiracy theories a reality. Trump continues to claim millions of non-citizen voters are participating in federal elections — something he persists in proclaiming despite having won two of the last three presidential races.This isn’t really about Trump as much as it is about convincing as many people as possible that any election results Trump doesn’t like must be the result of illegal activity. This has led to the DOJ raiding election offices and the DHS claiming (with no facts in evidence) that there are hundreds of thousands of people across the United States who are illegally registered to vote.Any cursory investigation of the administration’s claims have immediately proven them to be false. And that appears to have altered the administration’s tactics. It’s no longer willing to make wild claims about voter registries. It is now engaging in almost immediate lawfare if its targets don’t immediately bend the knee and kowtow to whatever demands the administration is making. The complaint [PDF] filed by the DOJ insists California is illegally registering non-citizens for voting and then allowing them to vote. But before we get to the complaint, let’s hang back and take a closer look at the clown squad that now presents itself as Trump’s Department of Justice, as delivered here by NPR:On Tuesday, three weeks before Election Day, the Justice Department delivered a flash drive to the top voting official in Los Angeles County. That official was told he had 48 hours to investigate names listed on that drive or he would be sued.So this thumb drive included the names of 20,000 people that the federal government believes are likely noncitizens and on the voter rolls in California. But LA County did not consider this drive to be a secure medium for this sort of information. I mean, the password for the drive was literally included on a Post-it note with the delivery of it. And the clerk there, Dean Logan, noted that. Also, he told the DOJ he felt the process that they were asking for would actually break numerous other laws that govern how elections run, including restrictions on voter purges this close to Election Day.So, this doesn’t look like the end result of a competent investigation by government professionals. Instead, it looks like a half-assed, poorly thought-out attempt at extortion. And the timing makes it seem even more suspect, given that the DOJ has had the entirety of its existence to create a voter fraud case against California. When you instruct partisan hacks masquerading as DOJ professionals engage in a rush hit job mean to keep California from (yet again) electing more Democrats than Republicans during an impending election, this is the absolute peak of competence you should expect.The lawsuit is just the DOJ carrying out its threat — the one delivered alongside a thumb drive and password-laden Post-It note. The DOJ claims it gave California election officials plenty of time to investigate the people it stated were registered to vote illegally. Then it claims that its failure to do so in this extremely compressed time period is evidence of California’s refusal to cooperate with a federal investigation.What it wants the court to do is force California to prevent any votes associated with this list from being counted until the DOJ has a chance to look them over. The very real result of this demand is that up to 20,000 votes simply won’t be counted following the mid-term elections, especially if the Trump DOJ doesn’t like who these voters voted for. The DOJ claims blocking these from being counted pending an investigation would prevent “dilution” of the vote. But that’s exactly what it wants to happen: the removal of votes it thinks might go to candidates that aren’t part of Trump’s MAGA platform. Given the timing, it seems the DOJ is headed towards an injunction blocking it from blocking these votes from being counted. But stranger things have happened, even in a judicial circuit (the Ninth) that is less likely to side with government than the people, no matter which party has control of the government at that point in time. But the threat will always exist as long as this administration is in power. The DOJ will do Trump’s bidding, even if it means destroying what little remains of its reputation, all in service of future illegitimate seizures of power.

item.title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
item.author: Rindala Alajaji
item.content:encoded: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for more than 50 years, and in the U.S. since 1998), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime.In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance.Understandably, the public backlash to police ALPR technology is accelerating, and state lawmakers across the country are taking action.This is a good start, but far more is needed. This blog presents a framework for state legislators who want to stop ALPR mass police surveillance:Just ban it. It is incompatible with a free society and cannot be fixed.In the absence of a flat ban, reduce its harms. Most importantly: limit police use of ALPRs to real-time comparison of passing plates to hotlists; require a warrant to place a plate on a hotlist; impose strict limits on the creation and use of those hotlists; and prohibit the storage of ALPR data (and thus prevent the subsequent search and disclosure of that data).In the absence of a prohibition on storing ALPR data, reduce its harms. Most importantly, place strict limits on police storage, search, and disclosure of ALPR data.Ban three especially dangerous police practices: placement of ALPRs near sensitive locations like hospitals; purchase of ALPR data; and use of ALPR data to try to predict crime.Require transparency about ALPR mass surveillance, including: a 30-day public notice before a city procures police ALPRs; a statewide registry of all police ALPRs; and regular, public audits and statistical reports about police usage.Ensure effective enforcement of all new ALPR restraints, including by means of a private right of action and the exclusionary rule.These policy battles often unfold locally, so state legislators must ensure that state law is a regulatory floor, never a ceiling. State preemption should never force unwanted camera networks onto communities that have chosen to reject them. Local government must retain authority to enact full bans, deny funding, reject contracts, and decommission existing camera networks.As in our previous post on ALPR policy, our focus here is ALPR mass surveillance: the continuous dragnet collection and retention of location data on innocent drivers. Different issues are raised by automated traffic enforcement (ATE) systems, such as standalone red-light or speed cameras that solely photograph and ticket specific traffic violations, without building a searchable network about uninvolved drivers. As such, state laws against ALPR mass surveillance should not cover ATE. This is the approach in at least six states: Connecticut, Minnesota, North Carolina, Oregon, Virginia, and Washington. The most common approach is to exclude ATE from the law’s definition of “ALPR.”Of course, ATE carries risks and demands legal restrictions too. This includes tight limits on data collection, retention, usage, and disclosure—all of which should be addressed in a different statute. Lawmakers must also actively guard against vendor efforts to piggyback mass surveillance tools onto ATE contracts.The Gold Standard: Statewide Bans on ALPR Mass SurveillanceStatutory limits cannot make ALPR mass surveillance safe. Because the technology relies on the indiscriminate recording of every driver’s movements, the risks are baked into the system itself. Also, innocent motorists will be menaced by police due to false matches, bad actors will misuse location data, and sensitive personal movements will be exposed to broad government overreach. Promising harsher penalties for officer misuse cannot fix an inherently flawed architecture. Thus, state lawmakers should pursue a complete, statewide ban on ALPR mass surveillance. lawmakers should prohibit all state-level law enforcement agencies from acquiring, retaining, accessing, or using ALPRs or any data derived from them. they must impose the same prohibition on county, municipal, and other local law enforcement agencies.These prohibitions should require any agency ending an ALPR program (both state and local) to fully decommission the programs within a strict timeframe. This includes requiring agencies to: physically remove all camera hardware; revoke all user, network, and database access credentials; permanently delete all stored location data; and require vendor certification of compliance. ban the use of state funds for state or local agencies to acquire, maintain, or access ALPR systems. This must include direct appropriations, law enforcement grants, pass-through funds, and state-administered federal funds. In August 2026, Texas Governor Greg Abbott banned state agencies from spending public funds on Flock cameras. ban state and local agencies from installing or operating ALPRs on state-owned highways, roadways, or public properties. In August 2026, Florida’s Department of Transportation ordered the removal of all ALPRs from the right-of-way on state highways within 30 days. The order revokes all previously approved permits to install ALPRs, and bars future permits.An outright prohibition is the only effective way to eliminate this mass surveillance. This follows the lead of municipalities across the country that have already enacted bans. However, where there’s political resistance, state lawmakers might consider a moratorium that prevents further expansion of ALPR networks.Strict Limits on Real-time Use of ALPRsIn the absence of a ban on police ALPR mass surveillance, state legislators must restrict ALPRs to real-time comparison of passing plates to hotlists. ALPR data is simply too dangerous for police to safely store, search, and disclose. An effective way to do this, as in New Hampshire, is to require deletion of ALPR data within three minutes after collection. That means no ALPR data is stored after comparison to a hotlist, and thus that no ALPR data about unmatched cars can be searched or disclosed.A state legislature must also reduce the harms of police use of real-time ALPRs by strictly limiting the creation and use of law enforcement hotlists.Limits on creating hotlistsRoughly speaking, there are two kinds of police hotlists. An agency might link its ALPRs to external hotlists created by another agency, such as the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC) or a state’s department of motor vehicles. Also, a police agency might link its ALPRs to its own internal hotlist, created by its own officers, of people under investigation. State legislators must strictly limit both., limit the kinds of external hotlists that police agencies may link to. For example, ban police agencies from linking to the NCIC’s “immigration violator” hotlist, which ICE uses to hunt immigrants with the ALPRs operated by police agencies across the country., if a police agency links to external hotlists, require the agency to update that link every day. Otherwise, drivers may be detained even though they have been removed from the list. This is required by Montana, Nebraska, North Carolina, and Virginia., forbid officers from adding a plate on a hotlist, absent a warrant from a judge based on probable cause and particularity. Without this judicial check on police power, an officer stalked a potential romantic partner by placing her plate on a hotlist.As with other laws requiring a warrant (such as the federal Wiretap Act), there should be an exception where: (1) there is an emergency involving immediate danger of death or serious bodily injury to a person; (2) there is no time to acquire a warrant; and (3) there are grounds upon which a warrant could be granted. This exception might apply, for example, when police have probable cause to believe a child has just been abducted. In such cases, the statute must require police to seek a warrant within 48 hours, and if it is denied, to immediately remove the plate from the hotlist.Minnesota requires a warrant or an emergency to use ALPRs “to monitor or track an individual who is the subject of an active criminal investigation.” In Maine, an ALPR system may use only information based on reasonable suspicion., forbid officers from adding a plate to a hotlist, except in connection with a serious violent crime. This would include investigation of a murder but not pursuit of a traffic scofflaw., forbid officers from adding a plate on a hotlist based, in whole or in part, on: a person’s race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, immigration status, disability, sex, gender identity, or sexual orientation; their political beliefs, associations, or participation in First Amendment-protected activity; or their pursuit of reproductive, gender-affirming, or other health care. Connecticut and Washington forbid use of ALPR systems on these grounds, and Virginia forbids tracking a person based on their protected speech., require officers to log their entry of a plate into a hotlist. This must include the officer’s name and agency, the date of the entry, a narrative description of the reasons for the entry, any case numbers, and an upload of the warrant authorizing the entry. Oregon requires an officer to log “the specific law enforcement purpose of the entry,” and the officer’s name., if the plate of a passing car does not match a hotlist, laws must require immediate deletion of all ALPR data about that car. New Hampshire state law requires deletion within three minutes. This is the most effective way to limit ALPRs to real-time identification of vehicles and drivers of interest to police, as opposed to amassing a dangerous database of the comings and goings of the entire driving public, available later for retrospective search by police., if the plate of a passing car does match a hotlist, then limit storage, search, and disclosure of its ALPR data to what is strictly necessary to the investigation that placed the car on the hotlist., require police officers, before stopping a car because of an apparent real-time match, to visually and independently confirm that the car’s plate number, plate issuing state, and other vehicle characteristics in fact do match the car on the hotlist. Many innocent motorists have been detained and menaced by police because of ALPR false positives. Confirmation is required by Kentucky, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon, Virginia, and Washington.Strict Limits on Storage, Search, and Disclosure of ALPR DataAgain, state legislatures should simply ban police use of ALPRs, or at least police storage of ALPR data. Third best is harm reduction through strict limits on storage, search, and disclosure of ALPR data., limit the storage period for ALPR data to days, not months, and then require deletion. More than 99% of the drivers who pass an ALPR are not on a hotlist. Tracking their movements anyway, just in case they are later relevant to a police investigation, is criminalization of the entire driving population. Thus, four states already require deletion after 21 days: Connecticut, Maine, Virginia, and Washington. Even Flock has reduced its default retention period to seven days.By “delete,” we mean permanently erase it, so it is impossible for anybody to access it again. It is not enough to merely store it in a way that makes it harder to access, such as archiving it, or transferring it from one database to another. In the words of the Virginia statute: “System data shall be purged … in such a manner that such data is destroyed and not recoverable.”, limit the types of ALPR data that can be stored: just a photo of the plate, the AI-based read of the plate number, the date and time, and the location. Conversely, ban retention of photos of people in the car, and of features of the car beyond the plate as well as AI-based reads of those photos (respectively, “facial recognition” and “vehicle fingerprints”).Many states have enacted such rules. New Hampshire bans ALPRs from “photographing or recording or producing images of the occupants of a motor vehicle.” Missouri bans integration of facial recognition into ALPR systems. New Hampshire and Montana limit ALPRs to “the sole purpose of recording and checking license plates.” Minnesota provides that “data collected by an [ALPR] must be limited to” plate numbers; date, time, and location; and pictures of plate, vehicle, and surrounding area., laws should ban “geofence” searches, which are searches in which police use ALPRs to identify all of the drivers present at a particular time and place, based on police claims that one of them might be the suspect they are looking for. Even a warrant cannot justify such general searches, because the Fourth Amendment requires warrants to “particularly” describe the person or car being investigated. These dragnet searches of stored ALPR data are the modern-day equivalent of the colonial-era “writs of assistance,” against which our founders fought a revolution to end.Three states (Minnesota, Vermont, and Virginia) require reasonable suspicion of a crime before searching ALPR data, and a fourth state (California) requires this from its highway patrol. This is a step in the right direction, but not enough: the decider must be a judge, and the test must be probable cause., officers should be prohibited from searching stored ALPR data, unless they are investigating a serious violent crime. On the flip side, ban searches for immigrants, protesters, or traffic scofflaws.Some states have moved in this direction. Missouri limits use of ALPR data “criminal justice” and “lifesaving efforts.” North Carolina bans its use for traffic enforcement. Connecticut bans its use based on race and other protected classes, to identify First Amendment activity, for immigration enforcement, or because of access to reproductive or gender-affirming health care. Idaho bans its use for political activity., police officers must be required to log their searches of stored ALPR data concerning a particular car. This must include the officer’s name and agency, the date and time of search, a narrative description of the reasons for search, any case numbers, and an upload of the warrant authorizing the search. The officer must write the narrative in their own words. A drop-down menu of reasons is no substitute, because it is too easy for officers to dodge an explanation of the actual reasons by clicking a pre-written “reason.”The “disclosure” limits below must broadly address sharing from an agency that collected ALPR data to another entity. This includes an agency opening its database to access and search by another entity. It also includes an agency transferring data from its database to another entity’s database., ban disclosure of ALPR data to any federal or out-of-state agency. Federal and out-of-state agencies often lack the necessary protections of the driving public. Connecticut forbids disclosures to the federal government or agencies in 46 states, unless they have a warrant. California forbids disclosures, unless otherwise permitted by law., ban disclosure of ALPR data to another agency, unless it follows all of the rules above for an agency’s search of its own data (that is, the ban on geofence searches, the requirement of a warrant, the limitation to investigation of serious violent crimes, and the requirement of an audit trail).Some states have taken steps in this direction. Utah requires, as a condition of disclosure to a government entity or a defendant in a criminal case, a court order finding reasonable suspicion of crime. Washington forbids disclosure “except as required in a judicial proceeding.” Minnesota and Virginia require the disclosing agency to find reasonable suspicion. Minnesota and Connecticut forbid disclosure unless the receiving agency follows the rules applicable to the disclosing agency., place strict limits on participation in a multi-agency disclosure network, such as Flock or Vigilant. Connecticut forbids participation “in a system or network that shares” ALPR data, unless it requires all participants to affirm in writing that they will not use or re-disclose that state’s data except in compliance with that state’s laws. Connecticut also forbids “bulk” data disclosure, and Maryland forbids data “upload” to another agency., ban disclosure of ALPR data for purposes of investigating acts and statuses that are lawful in-state. Three states (Illinois, New Jersey, and New Mexico) forbid disclosure to investigate immigration status. Two states (Illinois and New Mexico) forbid disclosure in investigate healthcare that is lawful in-state. One state (New Mexico) forbids disclosure to investigate protected assembly, petition, and speech.State lawmakers must ensure that the public has access to ample information about the ALPR mass surveillance in their communities. Many people will use this information to resist ALPRs., state laws should require local governments to provide at least 30 days of public notice before spending funds, accepting grants or private donations, or entering into any contract or pilot program for ALPR technology. All proposed vendor contracts and funding sources must be publicly disclosed prior to approval. This helps local officials to exercise their procurementpower to reject ALPRs., laws should mandate the creation of a centralized, public-facing state registry of all police agencies using ALPRs, and the specific locations of all police ALPRs. Sources like DeFlock and EFF’s Atlas of Surveillance include crowd-sourced maps of ALPR technologies, but they are not exhaustive. This was one of the provisions in Minnesota Minn. Stat. § 13.824, which in part, requires police agencies to notify the state within 10 days of installing any ALPR, and requires a state agency to aggregate this information and publish a master list of the locations of all ALPRs (unless a judge determines that disclosure of a particular ALPR’s location poses a genuine security risk)., mandate regular, independent, public audits of agency ALPR use, access logs, and query justifications to ensure compliance with all applicable laws and policies. Five states (Idaho, Minnesota, Montana, Virginia, and Washington) require regular audits, ranging in frequency from monthly to biennial. Three states (Idaho, Maryland, and Washington) require audits of access logs. Minnesota requires an independent auditor and public access to the results., laws must require each agency operating an ALPR system to publish regular reports on its website detailing key operational metrics. Six states require such reports annually: Connecticut, Maryland, New Hampshire, New Mexico, and Vermont. Arkansas requires them twice per year, and Oregon requires them monthly. These states variously require reporting of: the number of ALPRs, and a list of the locations of fixed ALPRs; the number of hotlists used, and a list of them; the number of plates scanned; the number of apparent matches to hotlists, and how many were actual matches; the number plate reads stored; and the number of searches of stored data, broken down by the purpose and agency of search., any new ALPR legislation must maintain a proper balance between transparency and privacy in the use of public record acts (PRAs) to obtain ALPR information. Public records and public scrutiny of ALPR programs have shown that people are harmed by these systems. So lawmakers should not cut off access to public records that document these abuses. For example, the public should have access to operational policies, audit logs, vendor communications, and aggregate statistics. EFF opposes blanket exemptions from PRAs that block public oversight of APRs—such as recent bills in states like Arizona. The better approach to protecting individual location privacy is a flexible, case-by-case balancing test already provided by many PRAs. Also, when a document contains both exempt and non-exempt information—like an audit log that contains both motorists’ plate numbers and officers’ search reasons—open records laws should require disclosure of the latter while withholding of the former.State lawmakers should adopt three additional bans to curtail the footprint of police ALPR surveillance., ban the placement of ALPRs or the collection of ALPR data near healthcare facilities, immigration services, schools, places of worship, courthouses, food banks, and other sensitive locations. Washington and Connecticut do this., ban police from purchasing ALPR data. Utah and Washington do so. Also, prohibit police from acquiring ALPR data from a private entity, except by means of a warrant. Washington does so. Utah took a step in this direction, requiring a court order based on reasonable suspicion. Absent this type of rule, police evade limits on seizing data from third parties by simply purchasing it from brokers., ban police and their vendors from using ALPRs or stored ALPR data to power predictive policing technology. EFF opposes such technology and urges state legislatures to ban it. ALPR companies have been providing law enforcement clients with an “analytics” feature, which ingests data from across police agencies, and produces a report of alleged crime trends, hotspots, and corridors. State legislators should prohibit this dangerous use of ALPR systems and data.A law without strong enforcement is just a piece of paper. EFF recommends three kinds of enforcement measures, all of which appear in existing ALPR statutes., all privacy laws need a “private right of action,” meaning ordinary people can sue a police department that breaks the law. An excellent model appears in the federal Wiretap Act. It expressly authorizes a lawsuit by “any person” whose personal information is processed “in violation of” this law. Privacy harm is harm, and so a person should have their day in court, even if they cannot prove a collateral harm, such as physical injury or economic loss. Moreover, the Wiretap Act provides a full arsenal of remedies to a successful plaintiff, including injunctive and declaratory relief, liquidated and actual damages, and attorney fees.At least three states enforce their ALPR statute with some version of a private right of action. These are good first steps but need improvement. Washington comes closest: it allows suit to enforce all ALPR rules and provides all remedies. Unfortunately, the plaintiff must prove “injury,” which may shut the courthouse doors to some people whose data is unlawfully processed. Connecticut allows suit by a person “aggrieved” by violation of some ALPR rules. But a person should be able to enforce all rules, and should not have to prove they were aggrieved. Oregon allows suit against a police vendor that “intentionally or with gross negligence” uses or discloses ALPR data in an unlawful manner. But this does not allow any suit against police, or even against a vendor that systematically violates the rules through ordinary negligence., privacy laws applicable to the police commonly ensure enforcement through the “exclusionary rule.” This means that if evidence is gathered in violation a privacy law, it must be excluded from court proceedings. This is sometimes called “suppression” or “inadmissibility.” The federal Wiretap Act has a strong version of this rule, clearly excluding evidence derived from violations of all rules. The so-called “good faith” exception hasweakened many exclusionary rules, so ALPR statutes should expressly reject this exception (though some courts have interpreted some statutory exclusionary rules to have no good faith exception).At least three states enforce their ALPR statute with some version of the exclusionary rule. Again, these are good first steps but need improvement:Virginia comes closest: “Any evidence obtained as a result of a violation” of some of the ALPR rules “is not admissible.” A better rule would apply to all ALPR rules.Connecticut provides that ALPR data “may be admissible … provided such data was collected or otherwise acquired or held or stored in accordance with the provisions of this section” (or obtained pursuant to warrant). A more clear exclusionary rule would “exclude evidence unlawfully processed,” as opposed to “admit evidence lawfully processed.” The exclusionary rule should also extend to data unlawfully used or disclosed (and not just to data unlawfully collected or stored).Washington provides that information obtained from “a knowing violation” of some of the statute’s rules is “inadmissible.” But the exclusionary rule should apply to all substantive limits (not just some), and to all violations (not just knowing ones)., police agencies and their private contractors that recurringly violate ALPR rules should be forbidden from using ALPRs at all. In New Hampshire, if an agency “repeated[ly]” violates the ALPR statute, the state department of justice may “seek an injunction banning [its] use” of ALPRs. In New Mexico, if a vendor “fails to comply with” that state’s ALPR law, it “may be subject to … suspension of authorization or termination of access.”Some states impose workplace discipline or criminal penalties on officers who violate ALPR laws, including Connecticut, Idaho, and Missouri. This is no substitute for the three types of strong enforcement measures above. ALPRs are a systemic problem requiring institution-wide enforcement of legal constraints, and not just episodic sanctions against individual officers.Mass surveillance ALPRs fundamentally threaten digital rights, making an outright statewide ban on police ALPRs the only effective way to fully protect privacy and safety. The next best thing a legislature can do is limit ALPRs to real-time comparison of passing cars to hotlists, by banning storage of ALPR data beyond a few minutes. If a legislature allows storage, it must impose a tight deletion deadline (days and not months), and strict limits on search and disclosure. A legislature must also ensure transparency and enforcement.

item.title: Cops Warned to Look for ‘Suspicious Behavior’ From People Opposing Flock at City Council Meetings
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock “may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target,” and told them to be on the lookout for “emotional confrontations” between people who oppose surveillance and government officials, according to a copy of the warning obtained by 404 Media.The warning, obtained by 404 Media, was issued by the Orange County Intelligence Assessment Center (OCIAC)—a government fusion center—in July to police in California. 404 Media recently obtained the bulletin using a Freedom of Information Act request.This surveillance bulletin to cops is the latest evidence that police around the country have been told to be on edge during public meetings where people are participating in democracy and utilizing their First Amendment rights about unpopular things the government is doing. We have reported on a spate of people being illegally arrested for extremely minor procedural violations or for cursing at city council meetings about Flock and data centers while participating in constitutionally protected activities.The warning is similar to others obtained by 404 Media and about the broader DeFlock movement and vandalism of Flock surveillance cameras. But this warning specifically tells police that there have been “no specific and credible threats found” related to city council meetings about Flock, but warns they should be on the lookout anyway. The warning noted that anti surveillance organizers could have been emboldened by the news that the Los Angeles Police Department ended its Flock contract, and may expect other local governments to do the same. The LAPD’s decision was “providing organizers and participants with a high-profile local example that could increase turnout and place additional public pressure on City Council members” to end their Flock contracts, the bulletin claims.“City-hosted events (i.e., city council meetings) may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target. Partners are encouraged to review for signs of suspicious activity,” the warning reads. This suspicious activity includes “excessive clothing,” “unusual questions or behavior,” people loitering,” or “unattended bags or packages.” The warning goes on to say that genuine interest in ending mass surveillance at a city council meeting “may present public safety risks,” which includes “large turnout exceeding room capacity,” “emotional confrontations,” counterdemonstrations,” “media presence,” “social media amplification,” and “disruption of council proceedings.” Here is a full excerpt of the portion of the warning about protected activities that could apparently “present public safety risks:” Large turnout exceeding room capacity: If organizers mobilize significantly more attendees than the council chambers can accommodate, this can lead to long lines, frustrated attendees, overflow areas, or delays in the meeting.Emotional confrontations: Because the issue involves surveillance, privacy, immigration concerns, and public safety, speakers and attendees may have strong emotions. Verbal confrontations between supporters and opponents are more likely than at routine council meetings.Counterdemonstrations: Individuals who support the Flock camera program or emphasize its crime-fighting benefits may attend and express opposing views, increasing the potential for verbal conflict.Traffic and parking impacts: A well-attended meeting can create localized congestion around City Hall before and after the meeting.Media presence: Local television, newspapers, livestreamers, and independent journalists may attend because the issue has recently received regional media coverage.Social media amplification. Attendees may livestream or record interactions. Minor disputes can quickly spread online, increasing public attention.Disruption of council proceedings. Possible issues include:Shouting from the audienceRefusing to yield the podium after time limitsCoordinated chanting inside the chambersAttempts to delay or prevent the meeting from continuingPhysical altercations: Heated disagreements between attendees with opposing viewpoints could escalate into minor physical altercations, particularly during emotionally charged interactions before, during, or after the meeting.Targeted threats or intimidation: Any credible threats, harassment, or intimidation directed toward elected officials, city staff, organizers, or attendees should be treated as a significant public safety concern and evaluated promptly.Extremist-related activity: Although there is no publicly available information indicating extremist involvement, politically contentious events may attract isolated individuals seeking to promote unrelated ideological causes.“The OCIAC recognizes that Americans have constitutionally protected rights to assemble, speak, and petition the government,” the warning ends. “The OCIAC safeguards these rights and only reports on First Amendment protected activities for operational planning in the interest of assuring the safety and security of the demonstrators and the public.”

item.title: Expert For News Orgs Suing OpenAI Warned ‘Always Verify’ AI, Then Didn’t Verify His AI-Made Charts In His Expert Report
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: A few weeks ago we wrote about how the lawyers for OpenAI and Microsoft in the massive multi-district litigation (MDL) against the companies over how they trained their AI had called for the exclusion of an expert witness report after it was revealed that lawyers for the plaintiffs had apparently surreptitiously paid for the report, and then tried to sneak it into evidence past the deadline for expert reports via a different expert who admitted he wasn’t familiar with the details of how the report was put together.There are so many filings in this case (currently over 2,100) that it’s difficult to keep up with them all, but around the same time as they called out that expert’s report, they also tried to disqualify a number of other experts put forth by the plaintiffs. Trying to disqualify experts isn’t that big a deal, it happens all the time. But buried in this particular motion was an incredible claim regarding Professor Oren Etzioni, a long-term AI optimist turned skeptic, who has been warning that AI will supercharge the spread of disinformation online.But in 2019 Dr. Etzioni, a University of Washington professor and founding chief executive of the Allen Institute for A.I., became one of the first researchers to warn that a new breed of A.I. would accelerate the spread of disinformation online. And by the middle of last year, he said, he was distressed that A.I.-generated deepfakes would swing a major election. He founded a nonprofit,in January, hoping to fight that threat.A word of caution that I can’t repeat often enough: always verify anything important yourself. AI models hallucinate. They fabricate quotes, invent statistics, and present fiction with the serene confidence of a tenured professor. The verification step is essential. If you skip it, you are not reading with AI. You are gambling with AI.Well… apparently Etzioni himself gambled and lost.News Plaintiffs’ expert Etzioni’s opinions as to the supposed importance of news content in LLM training should be excluded because they are based on now-withdrawn AI-generated charts… To support his opinions, Etzioni offered a series of figures that included hallucinated figures based on the cited academic papers….None of the numbers or measurements above were in the cited papers. Etzioni had used Anthropic’s Claude to generate the figures, which generated fake numbers. Etzioni admitted he failed to verify whether the figures were supported…. Etzioni conceded the charts did not meet his “standards for academic rigor,” … and following his deposition withdrew them. He also removed another AI-generated chart from his Rebuttal Report. Etzioni provided no other evidence to compensate, and his opinions concerning the value of news should be excluded.To have one expert report entered under questionable circumstances may be an error. But to have two smacks of desperation, and this is true even as these experts are coming from two different sets of plaintiffs in this case (and even after the publishing plaintiffs decided to drop that original report we spoke about a few weeks ago). This is a big case that could shape how AI gets built for years. When the plaintiffs keep leaning on experts this shaky, it’s hard not to read it as a sign that the underlying case is weaker than they’d like, and that they’re hoping to pressure the AI companies into folding anyway. It’s tough enough to fight a legitimate case. When the other side is so desperate to find experts to prop up their flimsy case that they end up in situations like this, it becomes even more difficult.Yes, there have been plenty of examples making the rounds of expert witnesses submitting hallucinated reports in multiple court cases. But this is a case literally challenging the ability of AI companies to read the internet, and to have one of the experts arguing against the AI companies get caught with hallucinated findings seems extra embarrassing.Indeed, you could argue there’s a deep irony with Etzioni’s reliance on fabricated data, beyond just his own warnings about it, given that if the side who retained him wins this case, it will make it that much more difficult to fight back against hallucinations and misinformation. AI tools that can read and retrieve content from the wider web, including news sites, can check and cite their sources instead of making things up. But the plaintiffs who brought Etzioni into this case are effectively trying to block that, which would likely leave us with less reliable tools that are even more of a “gamble” to rely on.

item.title: PHP Warns It Plans To Release 2 Emergency Patches Imminently
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Website admins, brace yourselves. Fixes for what are believed to be uncommonly severe vulnerabilities are scheduled to drop in a little more than 12 hours for PHP, a programming language that powers websites and Web applications everywhere. PHP maintainers said Monday that they planned to release patches for two vulnerabilities, both with severity ratings of 9.2 out of a possible 10.
"All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available," the advisory stated. "We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild." The maintainers published the advisory following the leaking of purported details, which have yet to be confirmed. The report showed a video of an exploit tool dubbed PHP2Shell executing code on webservers running WordPress 7.1.3, MediaWiki 1.46.2, phpBB 3.3.17, Magento 2.4.9, Joomla 6.2.0, Laravel 13.36.0, Laravel 8.83.29, Symphony 8.1.9, Drupal 11.4.10, and WHMCS 9.0.9, all of which use PHP. A video depicting the tool has been reposted here.
Attempts to locate the unconfirmed report were unsuccessful, but security firm watchTowr said it claimed to affect every PHP version from PHP 5, released in 2004, onward. The security firm went on to say it has confirmed that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are real. Researchers from separate security firm Sansec said they "expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release." A third security firm, Webfence, also urged admins to prepare now. Huntress has also issued an advisory.

item.title: The Chestnut Grove Caught in the Middle of A Years-Long Data Center Fight
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: Near the bank of the Ohio River, a historic American chestnut grove in Mason County, West Virginia has become the epicenter of a fight against a planned 2,250 acre data center campus. Plans for the UK-based startup Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus, with clients , Nvidia and , encompass the former Clements State Nursery and the American chestnut trees still growing there. For thousands of years, the American chestnut tree was a staple of life. Its natural range spanned hundreds of millions of acres from Maine to Mississippi, centuries before those names existed. As many as four billion trees provided a hearty nut crop for humans and provided miraculously rot-resistant lumber for railroad ties and housing. It sustained black bears as they prepared to hibernate, fed white-tailed deer and turkey, and shed nutrient-dense leaves. The largest American chestnut trees once grew 100 feet tall and 13 feet wide and represented one-fourth of all hardwoods; a squirrel could scamper along their branches from New England to Georgia without touching the ground, as . In 1904, a forester at the Bronx zoo noticed something alarming among their American chestnuts: The trees were dying , struck by a mysterious blight. , that blight — thought to be brought to America on Asian chestnut trees — wiped out the tree’s population to near-extinction. Since then, conservationists have worked to restore American Chestnut trees and breed blight-resistant specimens. Typically, threats to groves include pests, climate change, and the fungus that destroyed their ancestors. Today, however, a new threat has entered the picture: data centers. I first heard about the Clements chestnut grove after a 404 Media reader emailed me about it earlier this month, saying that the trees faced “potential destruction after November 1, 2026.” Social media posts called the threat “,” and claimed bulldozers are lined up, with headlines declaring the grove is “.” In the last few weeks, the plight of a grove of fragile chestnut trees trembling in the shadow of a data center has gone viral. Goldberry Grove, a local regenerative chestnut orchard, “They’re bulldozing the American chestnuts after November 1st,” sparking more outrage. In 2023, Governor Jim Justice a multi-billion dollar deal with Fidelis New Energy for a lifecycle carbon neutral hydrogen production facility, including the “Mountaineer GigaSystem” and the . Nscale the American Intelligence & Power Corporation, sponsored by Fidelis New Energy and including the Monarch campus, in March. “The citizens of Mason County are elated with the announcement of Fidelis New Energy selecting Mason County, West Virginia, for its multibillion-dollar state of the art carbon neutral, clean hydrogen complex,” John Musgrave, the Executive Director of the Mason County Development Authority said in Justice’s 2023 press release about the new data center plans. With construction of the campus underway today, citizens do not seem elated. In September, heavy storms neighborhoods nearby to flood, as runoff from the construction site sent water and debris into adjacent properties as a section of the site’s fencing gave out. The Department of Environmental Protections (DEP) “to immediately repair and strengthen the stormwater controls that failed, install additional erosion and sediment controls where needed, and take whatever actions are necessary to prevent similar releases from occurring in the future.”Nscale told local news outlet WOWK 13 that it would pay for the damage. Separately, the company is trying to buy out homeowners, but the people living there are resistant. “What they’re saying is one thing, but they’ve got to prove it,” one homeowner . “I’m staying. Fight for every one of these people.” The fate of the trees has been a conversation among conservationists in the area for years. The American Chestnut Foundation (TACF) raised the issue in its May 2024 monthly newsletter: “Several communications have been made with [West Virginia Secretary of Commerce James Bailey] and he is aware of the chestnut trees at Clements. He assured the WV chapter that the trees will remain and be taken care of by Fidelis.” The newsletter bulletin continued: “Mr. Bailey stated, ‘We value the chestnuts and will ensure that they are cared for. The state maintains ownership and control of the property, but if that ever changes, then the trees will be taken care of.’” The TACF noted that the future of the grove was “unclear.” Three years later, the picture is sharpening, as chestnut experts and the data center developers clash. Sixty-two years ago, the first seedlings shipped out from West Virginia’s newly-designated Clements State Tree Nursery. The nursery was once owned by Mark Twain’s grandparents. The West Virginia Division of Natural Resources bought it in 1961 and the Division of Forestry operated it for decades onward. The nursery sold seedlings of several varieties of trees and kept 15 to 20 chestnut trees that showed promising traits of blight resistance. In 2021, the reported that the DNR quietly ceased operating the nursery, citing funding issues. “It was never set up to make money, but it was also never set up to lose the kind of money it’s been losing in the past 10 years,” then-Division of Forestry Director Tom Cover told the at the time. Today, all of the American chestnut trees remaining at the former nursery site are infected with the blight fungus, Mark Double, a past president of the West Virginia Chapter of TACF told me. Many have died over the years, he said, but most of the trees still have sufficient resistance to have survived for 35 years, in spite of multiple infections. “The WV chapter of The American Chestnut Foundation has been harvesting nuts from this orchard for more than a decade,” Double told me over email. Nscale’s Monarch campus is one of two data center projects planned for the area. Project Tamarack, which is owned by Starwood Digital Ventures, is planned for 10 miles south of the Monarch campus. West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey the project early last month. Morrisey promises 1,000 temporary jobs but just 300 permanent positions as a result of the project. that data centers rarely live up to promises about bolstering local economies. “Data centers do not bring high-paying tech jobs to local communities because they operate as infrastructure projects rather than traditional jobcreating businesses,” University of Michigan researchers wrote in a 2025 brief. “Although the construction of data centers can create many jobs, those are short lived.”Residents were stunned to hear that another data center was coming to their community, telling local news outlet WSAZ that they felt blindsided. Despite not being located on the former nursery’s site, the fate of the American chestnuts have forced Starwood to address it, too. I emailed Starwood on Oct. 8 asking if its campus threatened the trees. “I checked, and that grove isn’t on Starwood’s land,” a spokesperson told me. Sometime after Sept. 24, according to , Project Tamarack added a line to its FAQ section about the grove: “The former Clements State Tree Nursery is a separate property and is not part of the Project Tamarack development site. Project Tamarack has no ownership, control, or management responsibility for the property. Questions regarding the chestnut grove, the former nursery, or the property’s management should be directed to the West Virginia Division of Forestry, which operated the facility prior to its closure in 2021.” Nscale also claims that the trees aren’t on land it owns, either — yet. That section of land is technically still under a “plan to purchase agreement.” “We understand the deep community connection to the former Clements State Tree Nursery site, and we look forward to working closely with the Morrisey Administration—including the Department of Agriculture and Division of Forestry—and The American Chestnut Foundation regarding the American Chestnut trees while responsibly developing the Monarch Compute Campus,” a spokesperson for Nscale told 404 Media. They continued: “We want to be clear — there was never a plan to bulldoze the nursery or cut down the trees. Nscale does not currently own the former Clements State Tree Nursery but we are under a plan for purchase agreement. Once we own the land, we are focused on how to best care for the trees which, according to a recent assessment by an arborist, suffer from blight and adverse health conditions. We have always planned to incorporate the American Chestnut trees into the Monarch Compute Campus. As construction progresses, we will work closely with professional arborists and experts to determine how best to preserve and integrate them, covering all costs.”On October 10, Morrisey announced that the trees would eventually be moved, framing this as a way to appease everyone. “Under the preservation plan, the existing trees will be relocated to a more suitable environment within the property, potentially as part of an arboretum or integrated landscaping. That work is scheduled for late 2027, during the trees' dormant season, under professional arborist supervision,” the governor’s office .Amy Metheny, a forest pathologist for the West Virginia American Chestnut Foundation, that relocating the trees would inevitably kill them. “It’s my professional opinion that if the trees were moved they would die within two to five years,” she said.I asked Morrisey’s office if they’re aware that experts say the trees will die if moved. A spokesperson for Morrisey’s office replied: “We are aware of the concerns about transplanting and have discussed them directly with a member of the West Virginia chapter of The American Chestnut Foundation. The West Virginia Department of Agriculture’s assessment found that the trees are expected to continue dying under current site conditions. It also found that relocating chestnut clumps with proper care may improve their health, although some losses are expected.“Mature chestnut trees from the same original source as the Clements planting are growing in and producing nuts in Tyler County. Approximately 500 nuts from those trees are expected to be used for additional planting to support continued restoration efforts.“The company has said relocation remains its plan and that it will cover the cost. The property is subject to a legally binding purchase option signed in 2023 by the previous administration. We are working with the company and conservation experts to help secure the best possible preservation outcome. Specific questions about those relocation plans should be directed to the company.”Much of the information floating around about the future of the grove — including the claims of looming bulldozers, the timeline for the actual threat to the trees, the “not it” statements between both data center projects, and the governor’s promises — has been a game of rumors and conflicting information. A representative for Goldberry Grove declined to provide an on-the-record source for their claims of a November 1 deadline, or the bulldozer claims.But the attention turned to an otherwise largely overlooked and tragically rare tree species has stirred up the kind of public action that data center developers around the country have had to contend with when they want to throw miles of humming warehouses up in communities. On October 20, the West Virginia DEP hosted an in-person public comment session about Monarch’s air quality analysis and permitting, with a on October 29.The campus’s environmental impact could extend beyond the handful of trees at Clements, according to documents filed with the DEP. The reported, based on those documents: “Construction activities would result in permanent impacts to over 8,400 linear feet of streams and over 1.7 acres of wetlands on one permit and over 5,900 linear feet of streams and more than 26 acres of wetlands on the other, according to the applications.”

item.title: Broken Fifth Circuit Kills Massive Program That Helps Poor Rural Kids Get Broadband
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: You may have noticed that under corrupt Trumpist courts, if a regulator like the FCC engages in literally that threatens corporate power or aids workers, competition, or consumers (say, net neutrality, for example), or even school kids, it’s clearly illegal and a dramatic overreach of regulatory power.The latest case in point: the Fifth Circuit last week casually beheaded the $9 billion FCC Universal Service Fund (USF) program, which helps fund broadband connectivity to predominately rural and lower-income schools, libraries, and communities (read: a lot of Trump’s constituents). Bush-era appointee Judge Edith Brown Clement insists the FCC acted illegally by creating the long-running, bipartisan fund:“However, the FCC lacked legal authority in 1997 to establish the ​company, the Universal Service Administrative Co, to collect the funds and set contribution ​rates, said Judge Edith Brown Clement.“Because Congress never specifically authorized the FCC to ⁠establish USAC, we hold that the agency violated the Government Corporation Control Act,” she ​wrote for a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.”Quick background: the USF program applies a small surcharge on traditional phone lines to fund broadband expansion to unserved rural homes, schools, and libraries (of which the U.S. has a lot thanks to rampant telecom monopolization). With the death of landlines, there’s been a lot of debate about how to keep the program going (with, say, a small fee on broadband lines). While the USF, like all government programs, hasn’t been absent of fraud (it’s almost always at the hands of poorly regulated private companies), it’s generally done a lot of good for people stuck on the wrong side of the digital divide. It helps fund the kind of boring, steady infrastructure work that doesn’t get headlines or get mentioned in books about “abundance.”Enter Trumpism, which has been taking a merciless hatchet to absolutely any effort, anywhere across government, to try and ensure that Americans — whether rural Trump supporters, struggling school kids, or inner city urban residents — have affordable access to the internet.The USF is technically overseen by the Universal Service Administrative Company (USAC), which has been tasked since 1998 with overseeing more than $9 billion in broadband subsidies annually. Certain Trump Republicans had been pushing for the USF to be destroyed entirely, though that gambit was surprisingly scuttled by the Supreme Court in June of last year. That ruling ⁠overturned an earlier Fifth Circuit decision that the FCC’s funding mechanism employing mandatory contributions from telecoms companies had levied a “misbegotten tax” on ​consumers.With that avenue of destruction scuttled by the Supreme Court, opponents of having a federal government that helps human beings have instead shifted toward claiming it’s the USAC that’s illegal and government “overreach.” I should note, both efforts are being spearheaded by a dodgy Republican pseudo “consumer group” dubbed “Consumers Research.”The legal efforts to kill a popular bipartisan broadband subsidy program come as the Trump FCC under Brendan Carr have stated they’d like to dramatically revise or kill the program, something Carr has tried to claim is “a commonsense win for government efficiency and accountability.”I suspect the whole legal assault is being coordinated to provide cover for Carr’s planned “reforms,” of the program, which I’d suspect (based on Carr’s history) are being organized by companies like AT&T and involve ensuring that if any subsidies do persist, accountability of them is less than ever. I suspect the USF will survive in some form, though it will be shaped in service of telecom monopolies. The FCC could, for example, try to navigate the ruling by bringing USAC’s operations in house.This federal policy seppuku is then sold as “efficiency” and “policing waste” to a public that increasingly receives its “news” from a handful of consolidated corporations (only made possible by the simultaneous Republican assault on media consolidation limits and our corrupted courts). Great stuff. Extremely heartwarming.
